title: Stage II: Task II-B: Goals, Outcomes, Impact; Task II-C: Commitment
overview: Chapter 12 completes Stage II of Egan's problem-management model. It opens with the power of goal setting, drawing on Locke and Latham's research that goals focus attention, mobilise energy, prompt a search for strategies and increase persistence. Task II-B then helps clients move from possibilities to choices, distinguishing goals, outcomes and impact. Egan sets out flexible guidelines for shaping goals: outcome language, specificity, substance, realism, prudence, sustainability, flexibility, consistency with values and realistic time frames. He asks what kind and how much change clients need, covering needs versus wants, adaptive goals, coping, second-order change and emerging goals. Task II-C addresses commitment ('What am I willing to pay for what I want?') through economics, incentives, ownership, contracts and competing agendas, followed by Bandura's self-efficacy and ways to strengthen it. The chapter closes with Stage II as a trigger for action, Gollwitzer's implementation intentions, and the shadow side of goal setting.
objectives: Explain the four ways goal setting empowers clients and the idea of covert goals.
Distinguish goals, outcomes and problem-managing outcomes, and describe Task II-B as moving from possibilities to choices.
Describe and illustrate each of Egan's flexible guidelines for helping clients set goals.
Distinguish good intentions, broad aims and specific goals, and instrumental from ultimate goals.
Discuss how much and what kind of change clients need: needs vs wants, adaptive goals, coping and first- vs second-order change.
Explain Task II-C and the strategies for helping clients commit: economics, incentives, ownership, contracts and handling competing agendas.
Define self-efficacy, distinguish it from outcome expectations, and describe ways to strengthen it.
Explain how Stage II tasks trigger action and the role of implementation intentions.
Evaluate the shadow side of goal setting, including cultural considerations.

sections.heading: The Power of Goal Setting
sections.detailed:
Goal setting is part of ordinary life. Egan opens by noting that everyone sets goals all the time, whether or not they call it that. Quoting Dorner, he points out that nobody cooks a meal or writes a letter without some reason: we act to get what we want or to avoid what we do not want, and these desires act like beacons that show us which way to go. Once formalised into goals, they become central to problem solving.

Not setting goals is also goal setting. If people do not name their goals, they still have them; they simply operate with covert or default goals, which may be enhancing or limiting. Egan's example is the person who dislikes the flab in the mirror but never decides to get fit, which is really a decision to let fitness drift. Because life is full of goals, chosen or by default, it makes sense to make them work for us. At their best, goals mobilise our resources, are a critical part of the self-regulation system, and, if they are the right ones, point us in the right direction.

The research base. Egan notes a large body of theory and research on goals (Karoly; Locke and Latham). In a 2002 American Psychologist article Locke and Latham summarised 35 years of empirical work, which suggests that helping clients set goals empowers them in four ways.

1. Goals help clients focus their attention. Simon, a torture survivor seen at a London refugee centre, seemed aimless until his counselor, on her supervisor's advice, asked what one thing he would want that he did not have. He immediately said "a friend" and stayed focused for the rest of the session. His main concern was loneliness in a foreign country, and his fear that torture had made him psychologically unattractive.

2. Goals help clients mobilise energy and direct effort. Clients who are lethargic while exploring problems often come alive when discussing a better future. A listless rehabilitation patient decided, after a visit from her minister, that God and creation rather than pain would be the centre of her life, and she then cooperated much more fully with her pain-management exercises. Clients with goals engage in less aimless behaviour, and even broad or rudimentary goals can start constructive change; goal setting is not just a 'head' exercise.

3. Goals provide incentives to search for strategies. Setting goals (a Stage II task) leads naturally into looking for ways to achieve them (a Stage III task). Lonnie, a woman in her 70s, decided after a heart scare that she wanted to 'begin living again' and found ingenious ways to rebuild her social life, including low-budget remodelling and taking two college students as boarders.

4. Clear and specific goals increase persistence. Clients with clear goals work harder and longer. An AIDS patient who wanted to be reintegrated into his extended family recovered from five hospitalisations to achieve it. Payne, Robbins and Dougherty (1991) found that highly goal-directed retirees were more outgoing, involved, resourceful and persistent than low-goal-directed retirees, who were more self-critical, dissatisfied, sulky and self-centred.

A continuum of direction. Egan asks us to picture a continuum from the aimless person to someone with a keen sense of direction. Taz knows he wants to be a better supervisor and needs a programme; his colleague Lola does not even know if the job suits her and explores little. The same client can be at different points for different issues, and most people have directionless periods in some area of life.
sections.simple: Everyone sets goals, even by default. Research summarised by Locke and Latham shows goals help clients focus attention, mobilise energy, search for strategies and persist longer. People with direction turn wishes into specific outcomes instead of wishful thinking.
keyPoints: Not naming goals still leaves covert or default goals, which can help or limit.
Goals mobilise resources and are a key part of self-regulation.
Locke and Latham (2002) summarised 35 years of goal research: goals focus attention, mobilise energy, prompt strategy search and increase persistence.
Payne, Robbins and Dougherty (1991): high-goal-directed retirees were more outgoing, resourceful and persistent.
Clients lie on a continuum from aimless to directed, and can differ across life areas.

sections.heading: Task II-B: Goals, Outcomes, Impact: Help Clients Move from Possibilities to Choices
sections.detailed:
From possibilities to choices. Egan recalls a lecture point quoted by Wosket (2006): Stage I is about failed solutions (things people do that do not work), Stage II is about solutions as problem-managing goals, and Stage III is about solutions as strategies. Egan adds that he now has reservations about the word 'solution' because it is ambiguous. Once possibilities for a better future have been generated in Task II-A, clients must choose one or more of them and turn them into a programme for constructive change.

Creativity versus innovation. Task II-A is mainly about creativity: removing boundaries, thinking beyond a limited horizon and moving outside the box. Task II-B is about innovation, that is, converting possibilities into a practical programme for change.

The case of Bea. Bea, an African American single mother, smashed bank windows after feeling she had been refused a loan because of her race and status. Talking with her minister, she sees that she has become very anger-prone, that venting has bad consequences, and that she takes her anger out on friends and her two children. The minister helps her look at four options: venting, repressing, channelling, or giving up and ignoring the injustices. Giving up is not in her nature; venting only makes her angrier; repressing feels like another form of giving up, and she is poor at it anyway. So she explores channelling. She joins a political action group doing community organising, including work on inequities in the financial system. She learns she can channel anger without abandoning her values or intensity, discovers she is good at influencing people and getting things done, and begins to feel better about herself; 'the system' no longer seems a fortress.

Goal, outcome and impact. Because goals are highly motivating, helping clients set realistic goals is one of the most important tasks in helping. Egan draws a careful distinction: a goal is a concept; an accomplished goal is an outcome; and if that outcome has a positive impact on the problem situation, it is a problem-managing or opportunity-developing outcome. Bea's goal of channelling her anger became an outcome when she became an active member of the action group, and it was problem-managing because it replaced aimless venting and its consequences with constructive community work.

Figure 12.1 maps the three tasks of Stage II: II-A, designing a better future ("What are the possibilities?"); II-B, setting goals or outcomes ("What is my change agenda?"); and II-C, exploring commitment ("What am I willing to pay?"), all leading to ongoing action and problem-managing outcomes.
sections.simple: After brainstorming possibilities (Task II-A), clients must choose some and turn them into a change programme (Task II-B). II-A is creativity; II-B is innovation. A goal is a concept, an achieved goal is an outcome, and an outcome that improves the problem situation is problem-managing.
keyPoints: Stage I = failed solutions; Stage II = solutions as goals; Stage III = solutions as strategies (point cited by Wosket).
Task II-A is about creativity; Task II-B is about innovation, making possibilities practical.
Bea moved from venting anger to channelling it through a community action group.
Goal = concept; outcome = accomplished goal; problem-managing outcome = outcome with positive impact.
Figure 12.1: II-A possibilities, II-B change agenda, II-C 'What am I willing to pay?'

sections.heading: Flexible Guidelines in Helping Clients Set Goals for Themselves
sections.simple: Good goals are crafted through dialogue, not handed over. Egan lists characteristics of workable goals (outcomes, specific, substantive, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, value-consistent, timed), illustrated with Mara. They are tools used selectively, not a rigid checklist.
keyPoints: Goals are specific statements of what clients want and need, shaped through dialogue.
Nine characteristics: outcome-stated, specific/verifiable, substantive, venturesome yet prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, value-congruent, time-framed.
Each characteristic is illustrated through Mara and her father.
The characteristics are tools, not a step-by-step programme; there is no formula.
Skilled helpers turn them into timely 'sculpting' probes.

sections.heading: Help Clients Describe the Future They Want in Outcome or Accomplishment Language
sections.detailed:
Outcomes, not activities. The point of counselling is not discussion, planning or activity in themselves; helping is about problem-managing outcomes. "I want to start doing some exercise" names an activity. "Within six months I will be running three miles in under 30 minutes at least four times a week" is an outcome: a pattern of behaviour in place by a set time. Similarly, "get some training in communication skills" is an activity, whereas "become a better listener as a wife and mother" is an accomplishment, even if 'better listener' still needs clarifying. Outcome-stated goals give direction.

The past-participle approach. Helpers can encourage clients to phrase what they want in past-participle form: drinking stopped, marital fights decreased, anger habitually controlled. This is more than wording. Stating goals as accomplishments helps clients avoid directionless or imprudent action. A woman with breast cancer who thinks she should join a self-help group should be helped to see what she wants from it: joining and participating are activities, but what she wants is to feel supported. Clients who know what they want work not only harder but smarter.

Karl and Laura. Egan returns to Karl, an ex-soldier with PTSD, and his therapist Laura, who has helped him tell his story and challenge self-blame for his comrades' deaths, moving back and forth between Stages I and II. Peter, an ex-soldier who has managed his own PTSD, acts as Karl's 'buddy'. Karl says he wants a more 'normal' social life but hesitates because civilian life is a different world; he is comfortable with Peter but not fully with Laura. Laura asks him to describe bits and pieces of that world, without a total picture or deadline. Karl says he would like to see women again, not for marriage, but a special woman friend who sees him as an ordinary guy. Egan notes that such concrete 'pictures' are evocative and helpful.

From vague to specific. When Karl says he wants to be 'more disciplined', Laura asks what he wants to focus on. He identifies his sleep: he had been sleeping and waking whenever he felt like it to escape anxious thoughts, but now that his anxiety has eased, irregular sleep is just a bad habit and part of his aimlessness. Laura reflects that more discipline means a regular sleep schedule. Karl goes on to translate discipline into specific wants related to school, work and appearance. The dialogue moves between II-A (possibilities for a better social future) and II-B (goals as priorities), and with Laura's help Karl begins to design his future in terms of desired outcomes.
sections.simple: Goals should name results, not activities: 'running three miles in 30 minutes within six months' rather than 'doing some exercise'. Phrasing goals in past-participle form (drinking stopped, fights decreased) gives direction. Laura helps Karl turn vague wishes like 'more disciplined' into concrete outcomes.
keyPoints: Helping is about problem-managing outcomes, not discussion or activities.
Outcome = a pattern of behaviour in place by a certain time.
Past-participle approach: 'drinking stopped', 'anger habitually controlled'.
Outcome language prevents directionless and imprudent action; clients work harder and smarter.
Karl and Laura: concrete 'pictures' (special woman friend, regular sleep) make goals usable.

sections.heading: Help Clients Move from Broad Aims to Clear and Specific Goals
sections.detailed:
Counselors often add value by helping clients move from good intentions and vague desires to broad aims and then to quite specific goals.

Good intentions. "I need to do something about this" is a statement of intent: a good start, but it must be translated into aims and goals. Jon, who has realised that his family sees his overinvestment in work as being for himself rather than for them, says it is time to realign his priorities. That is a good intention. He might act on it alone, or he might need help.

Broad aims. A broad aim goes beyond intention because it has content: it names the area and says something general about it. Jon says family life is deteriorating because he is not around and that he must, and wants to, spend more time with his wife and children. He still has no picture of what this would look like.

Specific goals. Using probes such as "Tell me what 'spending more time at home' will look like", the counselor helps Jon say he will spend three of four weekends a month at home and work no more than two evenings a week. This is a specific pattern of behaviour, but it concerns quantity, not quality, so the counselor invites self-challenge by asking what he will be doing with the time. Egan adds that a client once told him that for his kids, quantity is quality; perhaps Jon's family wants a relaxed rather than intense Jon at home.

Instrumental versus ultimate goals. Jon's ultimate or higher-order goal is 'a good family life', which will look different across families and cultures. Spending more time at home is an instrumental goal: it is a goal because it is a pattern of behaviour, but it serves a higher one. Because instrumental goals are strategies for higher-order goals, helpers should check that clients can answer the 'instrumental-for-what?' question.

The shaping process. A bickering couple illustrates the progression: good intention ("We want to straighten out our marriage"); broad aim ("handle decisions about finances much more constructively"); specific goal (reduce fights, make mutual money decisions, set up a month-by-month budget and bring a trial budget to the next session). Sound finances and less conflict are goals in themselves, but here the budget is also instrumental to peace at home. Intentions, broad goals and specific goals can all drive behaviour, but specific goals have the best chance. Clients can be too specific if they get lost in planning details and crafting the goal becomes more important than the goal. Clients, with help, decide which parts of goal setting make sense for them.

Goal setting and evaluating progress. If a goal is clear and specific, the client can judge progress, and a two-way feedback system lets client and helper keep clarifying goals. Being able to measure progress is itself an incentive. "A better relationship with my wife" is too broad to verify; "socialise more with couples we both enjoy" is closer but still needs clarity. Counting is sometimes useful but not always necessary; helping is about living more fully, not accounting. At minimum, outcomes must be verifiable in some way: a couple may say the meanness has gone out of their squabbling, they listen and accept each other more and make more mutual decisions, which is verification enough without a scientific experiment.
sections.simple: Clients move from good intentions ('I must do something') to broad aims ('spend more time at home') to specific goals ('three weekends a month at home'). Instrumental goals serve ultimate goals, so ask 'instrumental for what?'. Specific goals work best and make progress verifiable, though clients should not get lost in detail.
keyPoints: Progression: good intention, then broad aim (has content), then specific goal (a clear pattern of behaviour).
Jon's case: from 'realign priorities' to three weekends a month at home; quality as well as quantity matters.
Instrumental goals serve higher-order or ultimate goals; ask 'instrumental-for-what?'.
Specific goals have the best chance, but over-specific planning can become an end in itself.
Clear goals make progress verifiable; measurable progress is an incentive, but counting is not always needed.

sections.heading: Help Clients Establish Goals That Make a Difference
sections.detailed:
Substance means being on target. Goals need substance, and in counselling a goal has substance to the degree that it contributes significantly to managing the original problem situation or developing an opportunity. Goals that are not on target are not substantive.

Vittorio and Anthony. Vittorio ran the family business; his son Anthony, after years in sales and a part-time MBA, wanted more responsibility, but his father never thought he was 'ready', and their arguing damaged the relationship. A consultant-counselor who specialised in small family businesses, having seen this pattern often (a conservative father, a pushy son), spent little time on the problem and helped them settle on a scenario: a 'marketing department' headed by Anthony, who could split his time between sales and marketing provided current sales were maintained; Vittorio would not interfere; they would meet monthly with the consultant, whose fee would come from increased sales. After initial turmoil, bickering dropped sharply, Anthony found new customers (whose product modifications Vittorio reluctantly approved), and sales and margins rose enough to need another salesperson. Years later Anthony left to found his own business, but the 'deal' made a real difference to both the relationship and the business.

Substance as stretch. Second, goals have substance to the extent that they help clients stretch themselves. Locke and Latham (1984) reported extensive research showing that, within reasonable limits, the more challenging the goal, the better the performance: people try harder and exert more effort, becoming motivated in proportion to the challenge. Even goals that cannot be fully reached produce high effort if partial success is possible and rewarded.

The quadriplegic young woman. After a car accident left her quadriplegic, a young woman was full of self-loathing and close to despair. With counselling, she came to see herself not as a victim of her own 'stupidity' but as someone who could bring hope to young people with life-changing afflictions. She visited patients in hospitals and rehabilitation centres and got some to join self-help groups. She told her counselor that the best thing she had done was to stop being a victim and become a fellow traveller, and that the last two years, though bitter at times, had been her best. Her goals were high but proved realistic.

Challenging, not impossible. There appears to be a curvilinear relationship between goal difficulty and performance: goals that are too easy are seen as trivial and ignored, while goals that are too hard are not accepted. This difficulty-performance ratio varies across people; what is small for one is big for another.
sections.simple: Substantive goals make a real dent in the problem and stretch the client. Locke and Latham found that harder goals (within limits) lead to better performance. But the link is curvilinear: too easy is ignored, too hard is rejected, and the right level differs by person.
keyPoints: A goal has substance if it contributes significantly to managing the problem or opportunity (it is on target).
Vittorio and Anthony's deal (a marketing department) changed both relationship and business.
Locke and Latham (1984): within limits, more challenging goals bring better performance.
Partly reachable goals still drive effort if partial success is rewarded.
Curvilinear relationship: too easy is ignored, too difficult is not accepted; varies by person.

sections.heading: Help Clients Formulate Realistic Goals
sections.detailed:
Stretch, but not too far. Stretch goals energise clients, but goals set too high can do more harm than good. Locke and Latham (1984) put it that nothing breeds success like success and nothing causes despair like perpetual failure; goal setting meant to raise motivation can backfire if it creates a yardstick that makes the person feel constantly inadequate.

Egan's definition. A goal is realistic if (1) the client has access to the resources needed, (2) the goal is under the client's control, and (3) external circumstances do not prevent its accomplishment.

Resources. It is pointless to help clients set specific, substantive, verifiable goals if the resources are missing. Rory, demoted after a merger, wants to become a consultant. Insufficient resources: he lacks the assertiveness, marketing savvy, industry expertise and interpersonal style, and the money to tide him over. Challenged by an outplacement counselor, he changes focus. Sufficient resources: graphic design is his hobby; he is not good enough for a technical design job, but he applies for a supervisory role in the design department, since he is good with people, scheduling and planning, and knows enough design to discuss issues. The move is challenging but realistic, and honing his design skills may open further career possibilities.

Control. Clients sometimes defeat themselves with goals outside their control, commonly believing their problems would be solved if only others behaved differently. Tony, 16, felt like a ping-pong ball between parents who used him in their conflict. A counselor helped him see that he could not control their behaviour but could control his reactions: leaving when they fought instead of trying to 'help', saying he could not know who was right if either recruited him, and building a good social life outside the home, which helped him weather tension at home.

External forces. Goals are also not under clients' control when blocked by forces they cannot influence. "To live in a free country" may be unrealistic for someone in a totalitarian state who cannot change its politics or emigration and immigration laws, whereas "to live as freely as possible" there could be turned into realistic goals.

The pre-goal. Mara can influence but not change her father's attitudes; only he can do that. Carlos helps her see she may need a pre-goal: she cannot negotiate with him unless he commits to a reasonably open dialogue, so her pre-goal is to get that commitment. How to negotiate it is a separate matter.
sections.simple: A goal is realistic when the client has the resources, it is under the client's control, and outside circumstances do not block it. Rory switched from consulting (no resources) to supervising design. Tony learned he could control only his own reactions to his parents. Mara needed a pre-goal: getting her father to talk openly.
keyPoints: Locke and Latham warn that goals set too high can breed despair instead of motivation.
Realistic = resources available + under client's control + not blocked by external circumstances.
Rory: insufficient resources for consulting; sufficient resources for a supervisory design role.
Tony controlled his own reactions, not his parents' behaviour.
Mara's pre-goal: secure her father's commitment to open dialogue before negotiating.

sections.heading: Help Clients Set Goals That Are Prudent
sections.detailed:
Realistic is not the same as prudent. A goal may be achievable yet unwise. Although Egan's model favours a bias toward client action, action must be both directional and wise, and discussing and setting goals should contribute to both.

The case of Harry. Harry, a college sophomore and campus radio disc jockey, was admitted to a state mental hospital after a bizarre on-air performance with grandiose religious themes. Counselors found that this pleasant, likable young man was actually a loner; on a large campus people assumed he had many friends. After discharge he came weekly for therapy. When he realised that his contacts with women were perfunctory and usually in groups (he had imagined a full social life), he launched a full programme of getting involved with women. It ended in disaster, because he had basic sexual and communication problems and serious doubts about his own worth, making it hard to give himself to others. He was rehospitalised.

The counselor helped Harry move past the sense of failure by focusing on what he could learn from the 'disaster'. Harry went back to problem clarification and new perspectives, then set more realistic short-term goals about getting back 'into community'. The direction was the same (a realistic social life), but the goals were now prudent because they were 'bite-size'. He attended church socials where a volunteer offered support and guidance.

Lessons. Harry's leap from problem clarification straight to action, without exploring possibilities and setting reasonable goals, was part of the problem. Paradoxically, his failure helped him see his difficulty with women more clearly.

Two kinds of prudence. One kind is playing it safe; the other is doing the wise or even heroic thing. Problem management and opportunity development should be venturesome, about wise and even heroic choices rather than playing it safe.
sections.simple: A goal can be doable but still unwise. Harry jumped straight into a big dating programme and crashed; later, smaller 'bite-size' goals in the same direction worked. Egan prefers prudence that is wise or even heroic, not just playing it safe.
keyPoints: Realistic (achievable) and prudent (wise) are different.
Action should be both directional and wise.
Harry's leap from clarification to action without goal setting led to rehospitalisation.
Same direction, bite-size goals (church socials with support) were prudent.
Two kinds of prudence: playing safe vs doing the wise or heroic thing; Egan favours the latter.

sections.heading: Help Clients Set Goals That Can Be Sustained
sections.detailed:
Staying power. Clients need to commit to goals that last. A separated couple wanted to reunite; they did, and divorced again within six months. Their goal was achievable but not sustainable. They might have asked what they needed to do not just to get back together but to stay together, and what their marriage would have to look like to become and remain workable. In discretionary-change situations, sustainability should be considered early.

One day at a time. Many Alcoholics Anonymous-like programmes work because of their one-day-at-a-time approach: the goal of being drug-free has to be sustained only for a single day, and each new day is a fresh start.

Vittorio and Anthony revisited. Their arrangement had enough staying power to produce good short-term results, reset the relationship and improve the business. It was not designed as a lasting business arrangement, because in the end Anthony's aspirations were bigger than the family business. Sustainability, then, is judged relative to what the goal is meant to accomplish.
sections.simple: Goals need staying power, not just achievability. A couple who reunited and divorced again within months had an achievable but unsustainable goal. AA-style 'one day at a time' makes sobriety sustainable by shrinking the time span.
keyPoints: A goal can be achievable but not sustainable (the couple who remarried and divorced within 6 months).
Ask not only how to reach a goal but how to maintain it.
In discretionary change, sustainability should be addressed early.
AA-like one-day-at-a-time approach makes goals sustainable.
Vittorio and Anthony's deal was sustainable enough for its short-term purpose.

sections.heading: Help Clients Choose Goals That Have Some Flexibility
sections.detailed:
Specificity versus flexibility. Goals often have to adapt to changing realities, so in uncertain situations there may be trade-offs between specificity and flexibility. Egan cites Napoleon's remark that a person who knows from the start where he is going will not go far. Goals that are too specific or rigid can prevent clients from seizing emerging opportunities.

Jessie. Jessie liked his work and company but felt like a second-class citizen, given dirty work by his supervisor and sensing prejudice against Hispanics. He wanted to quit for an equally well-paid job, but although the economy was booming, his industry was in recession and jobs for his skills were scarce. His counselor helped him choose a more flexible interim goal tied to coping with the present: using his time to prepare for a better job outside the industry within six months to a year. He volunteered for special assignments to learn new skills and took crash courses in computers and the Internet. He felt good about learning and found the prejudice easier to ignore.

Counselling as an organic process. Just as organisms adapt to their environments, clients' choices must adapt to changing circumstances.

Flexibility, tenacity and rigidity. Gollwitzer, Parks-Stamm, Jaudas and Sheeran (2007) analyse goal-directedness in terms of three characteristics that apply both to the goal and to the means:
- Flexibility: the ability to modify goals while keeping their original purpose intact, and to change tactics, within reason, when one course is blocked, ineffective or inefficient.
- Tenacity: the ability to stick with a goal, or the means to it, when the going gets rough.
- Rigidity: sticking with the original goal or action plan even when the goal is proving ineffective in managing the problem or the action programme is not working.
They therefore recommend 'flexible tenacity' in pursuing goals.

Mara. Carlos sees that Mara's plans will depend on whether her father relents completely, a little, a lot or not at all. If not at all, she faces very hard choices; if a little, she may need flexibility about the size or substance of her goals; one extreme option is living and working apart from her parents. Carlos helps her see that flexibility is not just compatible with but essential to the new identity she is building.
sections.simple: In uncertain situations, overly rigid goals can make clients miss opportunities. Jessie switched to a flexible interim goal of preparing for a new career. Gollwitzer and colleagues contrast flexibility, tenacity and rigidity and recommend 'flexible tenacity'.
keyPoints: There can be a trade-off between goal specificity and flexibility in uncertain situations.
Napoleon: knowing exactly where you are going from the start limits how far you go.
Jessie chose a flexible interim goal: preparing for a better job outside his declining industry.
Gollwitzer et al. (2007): flexibility, tenacity and rigidity apply to goals and means.
Recommended stance: 'flexible tenacity'; for Mara, flexibility is essential to her new identity.

sections.heading: Help Clients Choose Goals Consistent with Their Values
sections.detailed:
Ethics and values. Helping is a process of social influence, but it stays ethical only if it respects, within reason, the client's values. Egan defines values as the criteria we use to make decisions. Helpers may invite clients to reexamine their values but should not encourage actions that conflict with them.

Vincente and Consuela. Their son lies in a coma on life support after a car accident, with practically no chance of recovery, and they are in great pain and uncertainty. One option is ending life support. The counselor should not urge them to do so if it goes against their values; she can help them explore and clarify those values. She suggests they talk with their clergyman, and they learn that ending life support would not violate their religion's tenets. They are then free to explore other values bearing on the decision.

Contradictory goals and values. Some problems involve clients pursuing goals or values that pull against each other. Karl wanted a business degree but also wanted to earn a decent living soon. The degree would put him in debt, yet without it his chances of the job he wanted would fall. The counselor helped him identify and use his values to weigh trade-offs. Karl chose to work part-time and study part-time, and chose an office job over a better-paid construction job because construction would leave him too exhausted for school.
sections.simple: Helping is ethical only if it respects the client's values (the criteria they decide by). The counselor helped Vincente and Consuela clarify, not override, their values about life support. Karl used his values to balance study and earning through trade-offs.
keyPoints: Values are the criteria people use to make decisions.
Helpers may invite re-examination of values but should not push value-violating actions.
Vincente and Consuela: counselor helped clarify values and suggested consulting their clergyman.
Some clients pursue contradictory goals or values that require trade-offs.
Karl chose part-time work and part-time study, and an office job over construction.

sections.heading: Help Clients Establish Realistic Time Frames for Accomplishing Goals
sections.detailed:
'Sometime' means never. Goals to be achieved 'sometime or other' probably will not be achieved, so adding time frames adds value.

Greenberg's three outcomes. Greenberg (1986) distinguished immediate, intermediate and final outcomes, applied to Janette, who hates her passive lifestyle and needs to become more assertive:
- Immediate outcomes: changes in attitudes and behaviours seen within the helping sessions themselves. For Janette, sessions are a safe forum where she learns and practises assertiveness.
- Intermediate outcomes: changes that lead to further change. Janette gradually transfers assertiveness to work and social life, choosing relatively safe situations such as standing up to her mother more.
- Final outcomes: completion of the overall change programme through which problems are managed and opportunities developed. It takes Janette over two years to become consistently assertive day to day.

Jensen. A 22-year-old on probation for shoplifting in a court-mandated programme. Immediate outcome: overcoming resistance and building a working alliance with his counselor, whose unapologetic, somewhat tough caring made him see her as 'on his side'. Intermediate outcome: a change in his entitlement attitude (from television he had learned that America owed him affluence regardless of effort); he came to see that work plays a key role in most payoffs. Final outcomes: completing probation without further shoplifting, and getting and keeping a job that helped him repay the retailer.

Mini goals. Taussig (1987) discussed the value of setting and executing mini goals early in helping; achieving sequenced mini goals can make a dent in many kinds of problems.

No set time frame. Some goals must be met now, some soon, some in the short term and some in the long term. For a priest unjustly accused of child molestation: a 'now' goal was relief from debilitating anxiety attacks and keeping his balance during the investigation and trial; a 'soon' goal was getting the right legal aid; a short-term goal was winning the case; a long-term goal was rebuilding his credibility and learning to live with those who would still suspect him. There is no formula for the right mix and sequence of goals; helping, though based on problem-management principles, remains an art.

Agency, not a checklist. Not every goal needs every characteristic. For some clients broad goals are enough to kick-start the process and they shape goals themselves; others need help with specificity. The principle is to help clients develop goals with some agency, if not urgency, built in; one client may need help with clarity, another with substance, realism, values or time frame.

Box 12.1: Questions for choosing and shaping goals. Is my goal stated in outcome language? Is it specific enough to drive behaviour? How will I know when I have accomplished it? Will it make a difference and really help manage my problems and opportunities? Does it have 'bite' while remaining prudent? Is it realistic and doable? Can I sustain it? Does it have some flexibility? Is it in keeping with my values? Have I set a realistic time frame?
sections.simple: Goals without deadlines rarely happen. Greenberg distinguished immediate (in-session), intermediate (leading to further change) and final (programme complete) outcomes. Taussig valued early mini goals. Goals can be now, soon, short-term or long-term, and Box 12.1 lists questions for shaping goals.
keyPoints: Goals set for 'sometime' are unlikely to be achieved.
Greenberg (1986): immediate, intermediate and final outcomes (Janette, Jensen).
Taussig (1987): sequenced mini goals early in helping are useful.
Time frames vary: now, soon, short-term, long-term (the accused priest).
Not every goal needs every characteristic; goals need agency built in. Box 12.1 gives shaping questions.

sections.heading: What Kind of Change Do Clients Need and How Much?
sections.detailed:
Client-driven therapy. Therapy should be client driven: the degree of change is in the client's hands. Focusing on trivial issues should be avoided, but a complete personality makeover is an unrealistic goal.

The Colson example. Egan nonetheless cites Charles Colson, Nixon's 'hatchet man', jailed in 1974 for obstructing justice. He converted to Christianity and changed his life radically. By his death in 2012 he had written about 30 books, received 15 honorary doctorates for nonprofit work in prison ministry, prisoner rehabilitation and prison reform, won the Templeton Prize, and received the Presidential Citizens Medal. Colson seems to have been one of the '100 percenters', people who give their all to whatever they undertake.

The middle ground. Most change lies somewhere between a teenager upset over a lost girlfriend and the Colsons of the world. The sections that follow try to answer the question of how much and what kind of change clients need: distinguishing needs from wants, considering adaptive goals, valuing coping, and understanding second-order change.
sections.simple: The client decides how much change to seek. Trivial goals should be avoided, and a total personality makeover is usually unrealistic, though Charles Colson shows radical change can happen. Most change falls in between.
keyPoints: Therapy is client driven; the degree of change is the client's choice.
Avoid trivial goals; complete personality makeovers are unrealistic.
Charles Colson's radical life change after jail is an exception, a '100 percenter'.
Most change lies between minor upsets and radical transformation.

sections.heading: Help Clients Distinguish Needs from Wants
sections.detailed:
What kind of change? To answer 'how much change?' we may first need to ask 'what kind of change does the client need?' Sometimes wants and needs coincide: a lonely person wants a better social life and needs community to live a fuller life. Sometimes they differ. Goal setting should target the package of needs and wants that makes sense for this client, and discrepancies must be worked out with the client.

Irv. A 41-year-old entrepreneur collapsed at work and learned he had a mild heart condition and multiple sclerosis; his future was uncertain. He made his living developing and selling small businesses and wanted to continue, but it was too physically demanding. He needed a lighter schedule, since 60-70 hour weeks were no longer possible, and, having always ploughed sale proceeds into the next venture on the philosophy that the future would look after itself, he now needed to think about his wife and three children's financial security. Moving from the lifestyle he wanted to the one he needed was wrenching.

Involuntary clients. These clients often need to be challenged to look beyond wants to needs. A woman who chose to live homeless was severely beaten on the street but still wanted the freedom her lifestyle gave. Challenged, she admitted the core was freedom from responsibility, doing what she wanted when she wanted. The counselor helped her explore consequences and other options: could she be 'free' and not at risk, was there a trade-off? In the end the decision was hers.

Milos. A political refugee who had been jailed and beaten, Milos felt confused, disorganised and hostile (though he thought he should feel grateful) after escaping to the United States, and resisted help for two years because at home he had been 'his own man'. With a counselor he realised he wanted to re-establish links with his native land but needed to integrate into his host country. Both broad aims would be freeing. He spent time in the immigrant community (different from the refugee community), which had long kept homeland culture alive while adapting practically; friends there became role models, and the more active he became, the more his depression lifted. Had he focused on only needs or only wants, he would have stayed unhappy.
sections.simple: Wants and needs sometimes match and sometimes clash. Irv wanted his hectic business life but needed a lighter schedule and financial security. Milos combined what he wanted (homeland ties) with what he needed (integration) and recovered. Good goals target the right mix.
keyPoints: Ask 'what kind of change does the client need?' as well as 'how much?'.
Goals should address the package of needs and wants that makes sense for the client.
Irv had to move from the lifestyle he wanted to the one he needed.
Involuntary clients often need challenge to look beyond wants; the decision remains theirs.
Milos integrated wants and needs through the immigrant community and his depression lifted.

sections.heading: Help Clients Consider Adaptive Goals
sections.detailed:
BHAGs. Collins and Porras (1994) coined 'big, hairy, audacious goals' (BHAGs) for super-stretch goals, but Egan thinks the term suits business hype more than helping. Some clients do want big goals and believe, perhaps rightly, that their lives will not change without them. Even so, big goals need a bit-by-bit approach; dividing them into smaller pieces keeps them from seeming too daunting. 'Within reasonable limits' differs from client to client.

Adaptive goals. Stretch goals are often most motivating, but not always. Some clients make substantial changes, others take a modest approach. Wheeler and Janis (1980) cautioned against always searching for the absolute best: sometimes a satisfactory alternative is more reasonable, because the time, energy and expense of finding the best may outweigh the gain.

Joyce. A near-middle-aged retail buyer, Joyce centred her non-working life on her demanding, pampered mother and had turned down promotions requiring travel and longer hours. Guilt blocked change; she said being a virtual slave was less bad than the guilt of standing up to her mother. The counselor helped her experiment, for example taking a two-week trip with friends despite her mother's objection. No harm came to her mother and Joyce did not feel excessive guilt, but the relationship was not restructured. Still, she felt freer, for instance to say no, and this slack made life more livable. Her stance was in effect: a bit more freedom, without abandoning my mother. Life was 'a little bit better', though not as good as the counselor thought possible; she chose a satisfactory alternative rather than the best.

Other adaptive examples. Leahey and Wallace (1988) quote a client who, after five years of self-help books, therapy and postponement, decided she could just get on with life with whatever self-esteem she had; enough self-esteem to handle situations was good enough. Some clients accept 'surface' solutions such as eliminating symptoms: a couple reduces petty annoyances although the relationship's structure contains basic inequities they do not want to tackle. Some helpers would be disappointed; others would see these as legitimate adaptation to rather than change of reality. All these clients did act, changed how they thought and behaved, and felt their lives were better.

Strategic self-limitation. Robert Leahy (1999) frames reluctance and resistance to goal setting as 'strategic self-limitation'. Such behaviours set limits on change, because all change carries risk and uncertainty that are distressing in themselves; putting up barriers limits both. The client is in effect saying "enough is enough", unwilling to face more effort, stress, failure and regret. The tactics are ordinary: attacking the therapist, skipping homework, emotional volatility, a 'this won't work' mentality. Helpers may point out this 'self-handicapping', but it is still not their job to push a specific set of goals. There is a big difference between the best possible goals and the goals possible for this client in these circumstances.

The main point. Helping clients cope with adversity is not shortchanging them. When you help them adapt rather than conquer, neither you nor they are failing; there is no universal rule of success when it comes to outcomes.
sections.simple: Not every client needs huge 'BHAG' goals; even big goals should be broken into small pieces. Wheeler and Janis note that a satisfactory option can beat an endless search for the best. Joyce settled for 'a little bit better'. Leahy calls resistance 'strategic self-limitation'; helping clients adapt rather than conquer is not failure.
keyPoints: BHAGs (Collins and Porras) fit business hype; big goals need a bit-by-bit approach.
Wheeler and Janis (1980): sometimes choose a satisfactory alternative rather than the absolute best.
Joyce gained a little freedom from her mother without restructuring the relationship.
Leahey and Wallace's client: enough self-esteem is good enough; some clients accept surface solutions.
Leahy (1999): resistance as strategic self-limitation or self-handicapping; helpers should not impose goals.
Helping clients adapt rather than conquer is not failure.

sections.heading: Coping as an Important Goal
sections.detailed:
A definition of coping. A 2005 Economist article said then-Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice's task in the Middle East was to help conflicting parties adjust expectations without squashing hope. Egan says this is not a bad definition of coping. Choosing an adaptive rather than a stretch goal has been linked with coping (Coyne and Racioppo; Folkman and Moskowitz; Lazarus; Snyder). Everyone copes rather than conquers at times; in human affairs coping probably outstrips conquering, and sometimes the choice is cope or succumb. Coping has a bad reputation for some because it seems tied to mediocrity, but in many hard situations helping clients cope is one of the best things helpers can do.

The upside of coping. A young mother of three has just lost her husband. When people say she is 'coping quite well', they mean she is not letting grief overwhelm her, is caring for the children and helping them with their loss, and is handling the tasks a death brings. At that stage, little could be more positive.

Generating positive affect. Folkman and Moskowitz (2000) see positive affect as important in coping and ask how counselors can help clients generate and sustain it under chronic stress. They suggest three ways:
1. Positive reappraisal: reframing a situation in a positive light. Victor, recovering from motorcycle-accident injuries, saw rehabilitation as 'one big daunting glob'. His counselor helped him picture the end state (fully engaging in everyday life, even riding again) and separate it from the arduous activities that lead there. He only has to cope with part of it each day, forging a link in the recovery chain, and each week he sees something new he can do. He has low moments, but also positive affect that keeps him going.
2. Problem-focused coping: dealing with problems one at a time as they arise. Agnes cares for her husband with MS, a disease marked by unpredictability. She does not have to cope with 'his MS' as a whole; each day or stage brings its own problems, and the counselor helps her pursue realistic, attainable goals focused on specific near-at-hand caregiving tasks. Facing each problem gives her a sense of mastery and control, with positive affect that buoys her through the next stage.
3. Infusing ordinary events with positive meaning: in a study of caregivers for people with AIDS, Folkman and Moskowitz asked participants to describe something that made them feel good and helped them get through the day. More than 99% described such an event. These were ordinary things, such as dinner with a friend, flowers in a hospital room or a compliment, yet with the positive affect they produced, they helped people get through the day.

What coping skills does the client have? Suggesting coping assumes clients have coping skills: the thoughts and actions used to handle difficulty, such as confronting a situation directly and trying to change it, distancing oneself, controlling one's feelings and actions, seeking social support, and accepting responsibility while trying to make things right (Rexrode, Petersen and O'Toole; Roussi and colleagues). Even with a repertoire of skills, clients need flexibility to fit the skill to the situation and alter it when needed (Cheng; Kato). If clients lack the skills, helpers can coach them through the situation or, better, teach the skills, as discussed in Chapter 13.
sections.simple: Coping means adjusting expectations without crushing hope, and it is often the best goal available. Folkman and Moskowitz suggest three ways to build positive affect while coping: positive reappraisal, problem-focused coping and finding positive meaning in ordinary events. Clients need coping skills and the flexibility to use them.
keyPoints: Coping: adjusting expectations without squashing hope (Economist on Rice).
Choosing adaptive rather than stretch goals is associated with coping; coping often outstrips conquering.
Folkman and Moskowitz (2000): positive reappraisal (Victor), problem-focused coping (Agnes), positive meaning in ordinary events.
Over 99% of AIDS caregivers recalled an ordinary positive event that helped them through the day.
Coping skills include direct confrontation, distancing, self-control, seeking support and accepting responsibility; flexibility in using them matters.

sections.heading: Second-Order Change Goals
sections.simple: First-order change adjusts and fixes; second-order change transforms the underlying system (Singhal, Rao and Pant). The literature often treats second-order change as 'real' change, but Egan sees a continuum where minor change also has value. The client chooses, as Mara and Algis and Rodaina show.
keyPoints: Second-order change concerns how big or extensive change is; coping is the other end of the continuum.
Singhal, Rao and Pant (2006): eight contrasts, e.g., adjusting vs changing the system, symptoms vs causes, old vs new narrative.
Literature often treats first-order change as the 'little brother' of second-order change.
Egan: a continuum; first-order change is useful and sometimes the only option.
Algis and Rodaina: reducing squabbles = first-order; changing the relationship's terms = closer to second-order. Clients choose.

sections.heading: Emerging Goals
sections.detailed:
Goals that emerge. Goals are not always designed and set explicitly. They can emerge naturally through the client-helper dialogue or through the client's everyday interaction with the environment. As clients talk about problems and unused opportunities, possible goals and strategies often 'bubble up'. Once a problem is clarified through probing, empathic highlights and challenge, clients see more clearly what they want and what they need to do. Some clients must first act before they discover what they want. Once goals begin to emerge, counselors help clients clarify them and find ways to implement them.

What emergence should not mean. 'Emerge' does not mean waiting around until something comes up, nor trying many different solutions in the hope that one works. These kinds of emergence tend to be self-defeating.

Explicit goal setting still matters. Taussig (1987) showed that clients respond positively to goal setting even when goals are set very early in counselling. A client-centred, 'no one right formula' approach seems best: all clients need focus and direction, but what that looks like differs from client to client.
sections.simple: Sometimes goals simply surface as clients talk or act, and the helper then helps clarify them. But emergence is not passive waiting or random trial and error. Taussig found clients respond well even to early, explicit goal setting.
keyPoints: Goals can emerge from dialogue or everyday life rather than formal goal setting.
Probing, empathic highlights and challenge help clients see what they want.
Some clients must act before discovering what they want.
Waiting for something to come up or random trial and error is self-defeating.
Taussig (1987): clients respond positively to early explicit goal setting; no one right formula.

sections.heading: Task II-C: Help Clients Commit Themselves: "What Am I Willing to Pay for What I Want?"
sections.detailed:
Why commitment matters. After reviewing books on human evolution, Tickell (2005) observed with sorrow that while there is optimism about human ability to cope, there is pessimism about the human will to do so. Hence the need to address commitment.

A dimension, not a step. Task II-C is not really a sequential step but a dimension of goal setting, usually interrelated with the other two Stage II tasks. Clients may formulate goals without being willing to pay for them. Once goals are stated, the battle is joined: the client's 'old self' or lifestyle competes for resources with the potential 'new self'. On the positive side, history is full of people whose strength of will let them achieve seemingly impossible things.

The dying mother. A woman with two sons in their 20s was dying of cancer and expected to go at any time. She told her doctor she wanted to live to see her elder son marry in six months; the doctor spoke vaguely of trusting in God. Against the odds she attended the wedding, and when the doctor remarked that she must be satisfied, she replied wryly that her second son would marry someday. Counselors should not push clients to heroic efforts, but they should not undersell them either.

Commitment questions. Counselors help clients ask: Why should I pursue this goal? Is it worth it? Is this where I want to invest my limited time, money and energy? What competes for my attention? What are the incentives for this agenda? How strong are competing agendas?

No formula. Some clients race toward goals once set; others stop dead in the water. The same client may speed on one goal and drag her feet on another, or start fast and slow to a crawl. The counselor's job is to help clients face up to their commitments.
sections.simple: Setting a goal is not the same as being willing to pay for it. Task II-C is a dimension of goal setting in which clients weigh whether the goal is worth their time, money and energy against competing agendas. Counselors should neither demand heroics nor undersell clients.
keyPoints: Tickell: optimism about human ability to cope, pessimism about the will to do so.
Task II-C is a dimension of goal setting, not a separate sequential step.
Once goals are set, the 'old self' competes with the potential 'new self'.
The dying mother shows strength of will; counselors should not undersell clients.
Key questions: Is it worth it? What competes? What incentives? How strong are competing agendas?

sections.heading: Help Clients Commit Themselves to a Better Future
sections.detailed:
Initial versus ongoing commitment. Egan distinguishes initial commitment to a goal from ongoing commitment to a strategy or plan for accomplishing it. The proof of initial commitment lies in goal-accomplishing action.

Example. A client whose goal was a less abrasive interpersonal style began an evening 'examination of conscience', reviewing his interactions that day. He discovered, painfully, that in some interactions he went beyond abrasiveness to contempt. This sent him back to a deeper analysis of the problem and its blind spots: being dismissive of people he disliked or thought 'not important' had become ingrained in his interpersonal style. His action, in other words, both demonstrated commitment and deepened his understanding.

What counselors can do. There is a range of ways to support initial commitment and the action that signals it. Counselors can help clients make goals appealing, enhance their sense of ownership, and deal with competing agendas. The subsections that follow set these out as four headings: economics (goals worth more than they cost), incentives (appealing goals), ownership (embracing goals, including contracts), and obstacles (competing agendas).
sections.simple: Committing to a goal is different from sticking with the plan to reach it, and real commitment shows in action. One client's nightly self-review revealed contempt beneath his abrasiveness. Counselors build commitment by making goals appealing, owned and protected from competing agendas.
keyPoints: Initial commitment to a goal differs from ongoing commitment to a strategy.
The proof of initial commitment is goal-accomplishing action.
The abrasive client's 'examination of conscience' uncovered contempt and deeper blind spots.
Counselors help by making goals appealing, enhancing ownership and handling competing agendas.

sections.heading: Economics: Help Clients Set Goals That Are Worth More Than They Cost
sections.detailed:
Cost-effectiveness. Egan revisits the 'economics' of helping. Cost-effectiveness could have been listed among the characteristics of workable goals but is placed here because it is closely tied to commitment. Some achievable goals cost too much relative to their payoff. Asking whether a goal is cost-effective may sound technical, but the principle matters: skilled counselors help clients budget rather than squander their resources of work, time and emotional energy.

Eunice. Diagnosed with a terminal illness, Eunice learned that surgery, radiation and chemotherapy might prolong her life somewhat but not cure her. She examined what each treatment and combination would cost, less in money than in added anxiety and pain, and decided against all three because none promised much for the quality of the prolonged life. With a hospice-care doctor she developed a plan to ease her anxiety and physical pain as much as possible. Another patient might decide differently; costs and payoffs are relative, and some would value an extra month at any cost.

Understanding consequences. Because the cost-benefit ratio of a goal is often impossible to determine, counselors add value by helping clients understand the consequences of choosing a goal. A routine job with minimally adequate pay may meet immediate needs but prove a poor long-term choice. Foreseeing consequences is not easy. Another woman with cancer, unable to bear the sickness and depression of chemotherapy, abruptly stopped treatment saying she did not care what happened. No one helped her explore the consequences. When her health deteriorated she had second thoughts, saying there were things she must do before dying, but it was too late. Some reasonable challenge from a helper might have led to a better decision.

Balance sheet. The balance-sheet method (Chapter 13) can be used selectively to help clients weigh costs against benefits, both in choosing goals and in choosing programmes to implement them.
sections.simple: Some goals cost more than they are worth. Counselors help clients budget time, energy and emotion, and above all help them foresee consequences. Eunice weighed treatment costs and chose hospice care; another woman stopped chemotherapy without exploring consequences and regretted it.
keyPoints: Cost-effectiveness is discussed under commitment because of its close link to it.
Skilled counselors help clients budget rather than squander work, time and emotional energy.
Eunice chose quality of life over treatment that would only prolong life; costs and payoffs are relative.
Because cost-benefit ratios are hard to calculate, helping clients foresee consequences is key.
The balance-sheet method (Chapter 13) weighs costs and benefits of goals and programmes.

sections.heading: Incentives: Help Clients Set Appealing Goals
sections.detailed:
Useful is not the same as appealing. A goal that will help manage a problem and is cost-effective will not automatically appeal to the client. Setting appealing goals is common sense but not always easy; for many addicts, a drug-free life is not immediately appealing.

Karl and the crutch. A counselor working with Karl's resistance to giving up prescription drugs listens empathically and also challenges how Karl thinks about drugs and dependence. One day the counselor mentions 'giving up the crutch and walking straight'. Karl suddenly sees himself not as an addict but as a 'cripple'. He recalls a friend who lost a leg to a land mine in Iraq and longed to be fitted with a prosthesis and throw away his crutches. The image of throwing away the crutch and walking straight becomes very appealing.

What an incentive is. An incentive is a promise of a reward. Incentives help create a climate of hope around problem management and opportunity development. A goal is appealing if there are incentives to pursue it, and counselors should help clients search for incentives throughout helping.

Negative into positive goals. Negative goals, giving up something harmful, usually need to be translated into positive goals, getting something helpful. Karl found it much easier to commit to returning to school than to giving up drugs, because school meant gaining something: images of himself with a degree and a professional job were solid incentives. The picture of throwing away the crutch became an important incentive for cutting down drug use.
sections.simple: A goal can be useful without being attractive. An incentive is a promise of reward, and helpers keep searching for them. Turning 'give up drugs' into a positive image like 'throw away the crutch and walk straight' made Karl's goal appealing.
keyPoints: Goals that are useful and cost-effective are not automatically appealing.
An incentive is a promise of a reward and helps build a climate of hope.
Counselors should search for incentives throughout the helping process.
Translate negative goals (giving up something) into positive goals (getting something).
Karl: 'throwing away the crutch' and returning to school were strong incentives.

sections.heading: Ownership: Help Clients Embrace and Own the Goals They Set
sections.detailed:
Own the goals. Just as clients must 'own' their problems and unused opportunities, they must own their goals. The goals must be the client's, not the helper's or anyone else's. Various probes help clients discover what they want to do.

Carl Rogers. In a filmed session (Rogers, Perls and Ellis, 1965; see also Moon, 2007), a woman asks Rogers what she should do about her relationship with her daughter. He replies that he thinks she has been telling him all along what she wants to do. She knew what she wanted but sought his approval; had he given it, the goal would partly have become his. At another point he asks what she wants him to tell her to do, a question that puts responsibility for goal setting on the client.

Cynthia. Facing divorce, Cynthia told her lawyer she had decided on mutual custody, suggested by her husband's parents. The lawyer challenged her to start from zero and say what living arrangements she wanted and why, as he did not think it wise to help her carry out a decision that was not her own.

Why ownership matters. Goals suggested by others let clients blame others if they fail, and clients who simply follow advice often fail to explore down-the-road consequences.

From compliance to ownership. Commitment can take three forms:
- Compliance, the least useful: "I guess I'll have to change some habits if I want to keep my marriage afloat." It does not bode well for sustained change, though it may be better than nothing.
- Buy-in, a level up: the client accepts that changes are essential and must prove commitment. But buy-in, like compliance, may lack staying power because it relies too much on reason; "this is logical" differs from "this is what I really want".
- Ownership, the higher form: the client can say the goal is not someone else's and not just a good idea, but theirs.

The manager. Told by superiors that his career would stall unless he changed his style with his team, a manager first resisted, calling it 'hogwash'. Asked whether doing what 'they' wanted would cost him much, he admitted it would not, and moved beyond resistance. He identified areas to 'polish up'; within months, favourable responses from his reports led him to say it made sense and was the right thing to do because it helped people: buy-in had arrived. A year later he became proactive: delegating, giving and seeking feedback, holding managerial retreats, joining an HR task force and rewarding direct reports. He said it was actually fun: ownership had arrived, and his department saw him as one of the company's best executives. The process took over two years. He did not undergo a personality transformation or change his opinion of superiors who did not follow their own rules, but he changed his behaviour because he gradually discovered meaningful incentives.
sections.simple: Goals must belong to the client, not the helper or relatives. Rogers and Cynthia's lawyer handed responsibility back to the client. Commitment grows from compliance (weakest) to buy-in (logical acceptance) to ownership ('this is what I want'), as the manager's two-year change shows.
keyPoints: Goals must be the client's own, not the helper's or others'.
Rogers returned responsibility: 'What is it that you want me to tell you to do?'
Cynthia's lawyer made her 'start from zero' instead of following her in-laws' suggestion.
Others' goals let clients blame others and skip exploring consequences.
Levels of commitment: compliance, buy-in (reason-based), ownership (truly mine).
The manager moved from resistance to compliance, buy-in and ownership over two years through incentives.

sections.heading: Contracts as Commitment Devices
sections.detailed:
Self-contracts. Contracts that clients make with themselves can help them commit to new courses of action. They are promises to behave in certain ways and reach certain goals, and they also make goals more focused. Both the promise, expressed or implied, and the explicitness of the commitment help.

Dora. About a month after one of her two young sons disappeared without trace, Dora, separated from her husband at the time, grew listless and depressed. Counselling eased her guilt (she stopped self-blaming rituals), but she remained listless, shunned relatives and friends, kept to herself at work and distanced herself from her other son, Timmy. The only better future she would let herself imagine was one in which Bobby returned. Strong challenge from her sister-in-law, who shouted that Dora was trying to solve one hurt by hurting Timmy and herself, and that Bobby would never want this, jarred her loose. Dora and the counselor then discussed a 'recommitment' to Timmy, herself, the extended family and home. Through a series of contracts she reintroduced earlier patterns: opening her life to relatives and friends, creating a more positive atmosphere at home, encouraging Timmy to invite friends. Contracts worked for her because, as she said, she was a person of her word.

Acting into new thinking. At first Dora felt she was going through the motions, but she was actually acting herself into a new way of thinking. Contracts helped both her initial commitment and her movement to action. In counselling, contracts are not legal documents but human instruments to use if helpful; they often supply the structure and incentives some clients need.

The shadow side of contracts. No contract is perfect. Most people do not think through all the consequences of a contract's provisions, whether in marriage, employment or self-contracts. Even well-meaning people unknowingly add covert codicils, such as pursuing a goal 'until it begins to hurt' or not being abusive 'unless she pushes me to the wall'. These codicils are buried deep in decision making and only gradually surface.
sections.simple: Self-contracts are promises clients make to themselves that also sharpen goals. Dora used a series of contracts to rebuild her life and her bond with Timmy after her son vanished, acting her way into new thinking. But contracts can carry hidden 'covert codicils' that undermine them.
keyPoints: Self-contracts are promises to oneself that also make goals more focused; explicitness helps.
Dora's contracts restored relationships and home life after her son's disappearance.
She acted herself into a new mode of thinking.
Counselling contracts are human instruments, not legal documents; they give structure and incentives.
Shadow side: no perfect contract; hidden covert codicils ('until it hurts') surface gradually.

sections.heading: Obstacles: Help Clients Deal with Competing Agendas
sections.detailed:
Competing agendas. Clients often set goals and plan change without considering competing agendas: other parts of life, such as job, family and leisure, that soak up time and energy. The world is full of distractions. One manager wanted to build computer and Internet skills, but the daily push of business and a divorce drained his resources, and none of his self-development goals was achieved.

Rearranging priorities. Change programmes often require reordering priorities. A man who wants to be a full partner in reinventing his marriage cannot spend as much time 'with the boys'. An underemployed blue-collar worker may have to give up some social life for a more fulfilling job; she found a compromise when a friend introduced her to Internet job searching, which let her work full-time, search more effectively than by traditional methods, and still keep a reasonable social life.

Choosing between right and right. Not all competing agendas are frivolous. A woman expanding her horizons outside the home must still handle tasks at home; a single parent seeking promotion must balance new responsibilities with her children. These are questions of balance, not frivolity. A counselor who helped a two-career couple decide to have a child also helped them think through competing agendas once pregnancy began. A year after the birth they returned and said they had repeatedly reviewed that discussion of competing and conflicting priorities, and it had stabilised them for two years.

Box 12.2: Questions for evaluating clients' commitment to goals. Clients can be helped to ask themselves: What is my readiness for change in this area now? How badly do I want it? How hard am I willing to work? How freely am I choosing this goal? How appealing is it to me? How do I know I have the courage? What is pushing me to choose it? What incentives and rewards are there? If others are imposing it, what am I doing to make it my own? What difficulties do I have committing? In what way might my commitment not be true commitment? How can I remove disincentives and overcome obstacles? How can I increase my commitment? How could the goal be reformulated to be more appealing? Is the timing poor? What must I do to stay committed? What resources and support do I need?
sections.simple: Goals fail when other parts of life (work, family, leisure) eat up the time and energy needed. Change often means reordering priorities or finding compromises, and sometimes choosing between two good things. Box 12.2 lists questions clients can use to test their commitment.
keyPoints: Competing agendas (job, family, leisure) soak up time and energy and can sink goals.
Change programmes often require rearranging priorities or finding compromises.
Some choices are between right and right; it is a matter of balance, not frivolity.
The two-career couple benefited from discussing competing agendas before the baby came.
Box 12.2 offers questions on readiness, appeal, free choice, incentives, obstacles and support.

sections.heading: Great Expectations: Encourage Client Self-Efficacy: "I Can, I Will"
sections.detailed:
Self-regulation is the ideal. Clients need to find the motivation to seize their goals and run with them, and the more that motivation comes from within, the better. The counselor's role in client self-regulation is to help clients choose goals, develop commitment to them, and develop a sense of agency and assertiveness (Galassi and Bruch, 1992).

Expectations. Expectations also play a part in self-regulation; as discussed earlier in the book, client expectancy contributes significantly to successful outcomes. Here Egan looks at client expectations through the lens of self-efficacy, citing a large literature (Bandura; Cervone; Lightsey; Locke and Latham; Maddux; Schwarzer, among others).

Debate about self-concepts. Self-concepts such as self-esteem and self-efficacy, once taken as tried and true, have been questioned by more recent research. They have not been thrown out, and research continues, but the claims made for their uses have been questioned. Other researchers, such as Swann, Chang-Schneider and McClarty (2007), insist that self-views do matter and that it is worthwhile to develop and implement theoretically informed programmes to improve them.

Egan's position. Egan sides with those who see self-efficacy as an extremely useful clinical concept for constructive change. Concepts need not be 'pure' from an evidence-based standpoint to be clinically useful. His aim is to pique the reader's interest and help relate self-efficacy to helping, leaving the wider pro-and-con literature for later.
sections.simple: The ideal is self-regulation, with clients motivated from within. Counselors help clients choose goals, commit and develop agency. Self-concepts like self-efficacy have been questioned by research, but Egan sees self-efficacy as clinically very useful.
keyPoints: Self-regulation is the ideal; internal motivation is best.
Counselor's role (Galassi and Bruch): help clients choose goals, commit and develop agency and assertiveness.
Client expectancy contributes significantly to outcomes.
Claims for self-concepts have been questioned; Swann et al. (2007) argue self-views matter.
Egan: self-efficacy is clinically useful even if not 'pure' evidence-wise.

sections.heading: The Nature of Self-Efficacy
sections.detailed:
Definition. Bandura (1995) defines perceived self-efficacy as beliefs in one's capabilities to organise and carry out the courses of action needed to manage prospective situations; such beliefs influence how people think, feel, motivate themselves and act. People's can-do beliefs strongly affect their willingness to make an effort to cope with difficulties, how much effort they expend, and how long they persist against obstacles. Clients with higher self-efficacy make bolder choices, moving from adaptation toward more substantial goals.

Two conditions for action. Clients tend to act when two conditions are met:
1. Outcome expectations: they see that their actions will most likely lead to desirable results ("I will end up with a better relationship with Sophie").
2. Self-efficacy beliefs: they are reasonably sure they have the wherewithal (working knowledge, skills, time, stamina, guts and other resources) to carry out the behaviour that leads to those outcomes ("I have the ability to deal with our conflicts. I can do this. I'm going to do this").

Three illustrations.
- Yolanda, after a stroke, believes a painful rehabilitation programme will get her back on her feet (positive outcome expectation) and that she has what it takes to inch through it (positive self-efficacy belief). She enters with a positive attitude and progresses well.
- Yves is not convinced an aggressive drug-rehabilitation programme will lead to a more fulfilling life (negative outcome expectation), though he knows he could get through it (self-efficacy belief). He refuses, asking himself 'drug-free for what?'. He sees being drug-free as an instrumental goal but has no attractive ultimate goal.
- Xavier believes radiation and chemotherapy would help (positive outcome expectation) but doubts he has the stamina and courage (negative self-efficacy expectation), so he too refuses treatment.

Wider relevance. Outcome expectations and self-efficacy beliefs operate in everyday life, not just helping. There is a rich literature applying them to education (Lopez, Lent and colleagues; Multon, Brown and Lent; Smith and Fouad; Zimmerman), health care (O'Leary; Schwarzer and colleagues), physical rehabilitation (Altmaier and colleagues) and work (Donnay and Borgen).
sections.simple: Self-efficacy (Bandura) is the belief that you can organise and carry out the actions needed. People act when they expect the action to work (outcome expectation) and believe they can do it (self-efficacy belief). Yolanda had both; Yves lacked the first and Xavier the second, so both refused treatment.
keyPoints: Bandura (1995): perceived self-efficacy = beliefs in one's capability to organise and execute required actions.
Self-efficacy affects willingness to try, effort expended and persistence; high self-efficacy brings bolder goals.
Two conditions for action: outcome expectations and self-efficacy beliefs.
Yolanda had both; Yves lacked outcome expectation ('drug-free for what?'); Xavier lacked self-efficacy.
Applied in education, health care, physical rehabilitation and work.
