sections.heading: Helping Clients Develop Self-Efficacy
sections.detailed:
Self-efficacy can be strengthened in many ways. To show it is not a paradigm only for the weak, Egan uses Nick, a very strong manager who wanted to change his abrasive supervisory style but doubted he could ('I am what I am'). Simply telling him to believe in himself would have been silly; he needed to do several things to strengthen supervisory self-efficacy.

1. Skills: make sure clients have the skills to perform desired tasks. Self-efficacy rests on ability plus the conviction that one can use it. Nick read about and attended short sessions on 'soft' skills: listening, empathic highlights, feedback softer on the person and harder on the problem, and constructive challenge. He already had many of these skills, but they were dormant. Acquiring skills does not by itself raise self-efficacy; the way they are acquired must give a sense of competence.

2. Corrective feedback: base it on deficiencies in performance, not in the client's personality. Corrective feedback clears barriers to using resources. Egan, attending meetings with Nick, described the ups and downs of his performance, for example advising him that he need not respond positively to every suggestion but should sort ideas and show why good ones were good and bad ones bad, so everyone learns. Feedback that sounds like a personality attack harms self-efficacy. Helpers should ask how a piece of feedback will increase the client's self-efficacy.

3. Positive feedback: make it as specific as corrective feedback. It strengthens self-efficacy by highlighting strengths and reinforcing what clients do well. Often negative feedback is detailed while positive feedback is a perfunctory "Nice job", which sounds like a cliché. Egan described exactly how Nick interrupted Jeff's monologue, summarised it, used questions to show which parts were viable, and saved everyone time. The formula: here is what you did, here is the positive outcome, and here is the wider upbeat impact. Clients should see feedback as information needed to accomplish a task.

4. Success as a reinforcer: invite clients to challenge themselves to actions that produce positive results. Even small successes raise self-efficacy and give courage for harder tasks. Nick delegated minor tasks, his reports did well, and he decided to give them more. But the link between success and confidence must be forged: a run of successes alone does not necessarily strengthen self-efficacy unless linked to a sense of increased competence.

5. Models: help clients learn from others. Asked to describe the best manager in the division, Nick praised his competence and toughness; when Egan teasingly suggested he must be poor with people, Nick insisted he was excellent at the 'soft stuff', then realised he had been caught. Learning from models increases competence and self-efficacy, though it is tricky; Nick was too proud to think he could learn much from others.

6. Providing encouragement: support self-efficacy beliefs without being patronising. Support must be real, and what is supported must be real. Encouragement must be tailored to each client; what is supportive for one sounds patronising to another. A line like "Give it a try, Nick, I know you can do it" would have failed; Egan's encouragement was subtle and indirect. (Motivational interviewing and encouragement were discussed in Chapter 8.)

7. Reducing fear and anxiety: help clients overcome fears. Fear of failure blocks self-efficacy and makes clients reluctant to act, so reducing fear heightens self-efficacy. Nick feared messing up the business and making a fool of himself. As he tried new practices, results held steady and two team members became more productive. His fear of looking foolish was eased by noticing that outside the office, with field teams, he was upbeat and excellent at 'rallying the troops'; discussing his two styles helped him drop the fear.

Style. Egan admits he was Nick's coach and consultant, not therapist, and was mostly invitational rather than challenging. Helpers must adapt such a scenario to their clients; the chapter's principles are things you can do, not must do. Each helper develops his or her own style; no single style is right. A friend of Egan's, an excellent counselor who is totally 'for' her clients, does not tolerate nonsense and will say it is time to move on, and she is very successful.
sections.simple: Self-efficacy can be built: make sure clients have skills, give feedback on performance (not personality), give specific positive feedback, let small successes build confidence, use models, encourage without patronising, and reduce fear. Egan shows each with Nick, an abrasive manager.
keyPoints: Skills must be acquired in a way that gives a sense of competence.
Corrective feedback targets performance, not personality.
Positive feedback formula: what you did, its positive outcome, its wider upbeat impact.
Success reinforces only when linked to a sense of increased competence.
Models, non-patronising tailored encouragement, and reducing fear also raise self-efficacy.
Principles are things helpers can do, not must do; each helper develops a style.

sections.heading: Stage II and Action: The Tasks of Stage II as Triggers for Action
sections.detailed:
Goal work can trigger action. Formulating goals can itself prompt action: thinking about a better future often leads to experimenting with ways to make it real. Each task of Stage II has this capacity.

Task A as trigger. Developing possibilities frees some clients from thinking only about problems and lets them begin to fashion a better future; after identifying a few wants, needs and possible goals, they act. Francine was depressed because her aging, debilitated father, for whom she had put off marriage, picked on her with hurtful remarks, and her work was suffering. Her counselor suggested that the hurtful remarks were his illness speaking, not her father. This new perspective freed her to brainstorm answers to "What do you want for both yourself and your father?", such as both going through this with dignity intact and living the life he would want for her if his mind were not clouded. After brainstorming, her usual resourcefulness returned and she needed little further help.

Task B as trigger. For others, shaping goals changes how they see the future; once they know just what they want or need, they go for it. Nero, in his early 20s, killed his wife in a drunk-driving accident and was full of self-pity rather than remorse. His counselor asked who the most decent person he knew was (his uncle Saul), had him describe Saul's lifestyle, and then repeat the description substituting 'Nero' for 'Saul'. The contrast haunted him for days. He began to stop feeling sorry for himself, visited his wife's parents to beg their forgiveness, and began to see that there were other people in the world.

Task C as trigger. For still others, finding incentives for commitment triggers action: once they see what is in it 'for me', a kind of upbeat, productive selfishness, they move. Callahan, a small-business owner, faced a workplace discrimination suit from women, Hispanic and African American employees he called 'troublemakers', though he admitted they were good workers; in fact he underpaid them, and some of his mostly white male supervisors were abusive. A consultant suggested he attend a good diversity programme 'before some court orders you to'. Afterwards he said he had never considered the advantages of diversity, which had meant only politicians seeking votes; now seeing the business reasons, he knew some things he could do but still wanted guidance so as not to look like 'a soft jerk'. He remained a rough-and-ready businessman, but a package of incentives moved him toward needed action and might even have dented his prejudices.
sections.simple: Each Stage II task can kick-start action. Brainstorming possibilities freed Francine (Task A); shaping a clear picture of a decent life changed Nero (Task B); discovering business incentives moved Callahan (Task C).
keyPoints: Working on goals can itself trigger action and experimentation.
Task A trigger: Francine reframed her father's remarks as his illness and brainstormed what she wanted.
Task B trigger: Nero described his decent uncle's lifestyle, then substituted his own name.
Task C trigger: Callahan found incentives (business case for diversity) - 'productive selfishness'.

sections.heading: The Role of "Implementation Intentions" in Helping Clients Act
sections.detailed:
Commitment to action, not just goals. Commitment to goals is not enough; it must be accompanied or followed by commitment to the courses of action needed to reach them, which is the work of Stage III. Gollwitzer and associates (Achtziger, Gollwitzer and Sheeran; Bayer and Gollwitzer; Gollwitzer and Sheeran; Oettingen and Gollwitzer; Webb and Sheeran) have researched a simple way to help clients handle common problems in translating goals into action: failing to get started, becoming distracted, reverting to bad habits and so on.

Good intentions rehabilitated. Gollwitzer notes that good intentions do not deserve their poor reputation. Strong intentions (for example, firmly intending to study an hour every weekday before dinner) are reliably found to be realised more often than weak ones.

Implementation intentions defined. Implementation intentions are subordinate to goal intentions and specify the when, where and how of responses leading to goal attainment. They take the form "When situation x arises, I will perform response y!", linking anticipated opportunities to goal-directed responses.

Gwendolyn. A nursing-home aide, Gwendolyn tells herself: when Enid, a patient, becomes abusive, I will not respond immediately; I will remind myself it is her illness talking, and then respond with patience and kindness. Her ongoing goal is to control anger and other negative responses to patients. Because Enid is particularly difficult, she must refresh her intentions frequently. But her initial strong intention to substitute kindness and equanimity for anger means her responses become more or less automatic: the environmental cue (patient anger or abuse) triggers the appropriate response. In a sense, poor patient behaviour becomes an 'opportunity' for her chosen response.

Practical value. Helpers can help clients state strong, specific intentions that let them 'automatically' handle many obstacles to implementation. For instance, a person managing weight picks up a restaurant menu and automatically looks for the right kind and amount of food, ordering the vegetarian entree. The research on implementation intentions has great pragmatic value for translating goals into accomplishments.
sections.simple: Committing to a goal is not enough; clients must also commit to specific actions. Gollwitzer's implementation intentions take the form 'When situation X arises, I will do Y', which makes the right response nearly automatic, as with Gwendolyn and her abusive patient.
keyPoints: Commitment to goals must be matched by commitment to action (Stage III).
Gollwitzer: strong intentions are realised more often than weak ones.
Implementation intentions are subordinate to goal intentions and specify when, where and how.
Format: 'When situation x arises, I will perform response y!'
Gwendolyn's refreshed intention made her kind responses to Enid nearly automatic.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Goal Setting
sections.detailed:
Avoiding goal setting. Despite its advantages, some helpers and clients seem to conspire to avoid explicit goal setting; counselors explore problems and opportunities, then stop short of asking clients what they want. Bandura (1990) remarked that despite unprecedented empirical support, goal theory has not received the prominence it deserves in mainstream psychology. Bronfenbrenner (1977) recalled a Russian developmental psychologist telling an American one that American researchers try to explain how a child came to be what he is, while Soviet researchers try to discover how he can become what he not yet is. A main reason counselors do not help clients set realistic, life-enhancing goals is that they are not trained to.

Other reasons.
1. Too rational: some clients see goal setting as overly rational and sterile compared with their messy lives, and both helpers and clients object. The dilemma is that many clients would benefit from rigorous problem management, including goal setting, yet resist its rationality and discipline as alien.
2. Leaving the safe harbour: goal setting means moving from the relatively safe discussion of problems and their past roots into the uncharted waters of the future, which can be uncomfortable for both.
3. Ending victimhood: clients who set goals and commit move beyond the victim-of-my-problems game; victimhood and self-responsibility do not mix.
4. Demands on self: goal setting means placing demands on oneself, deciding, committing and acting. Saying "this is what I want" logically implies saying what one will do and accepting the price. Because this means work and pain, clients will not always be grateful.
5. Goals hem clients in: though liberating, goals also limit. A woman choosing a career may not have the marriage she wants; a man committing to one woman can no longer play the field.

Getting what you want. There is truth in the ironic saying that the only thing worse than not getting what you want is getting it. Getting what you want (a drug-free life, a renewed marriage, custody, a promotion, retirement, freedom from an abusive husband) brings responsibilities and often new problems. Even good solutions create new problems: parents who decide to give children more freedom then have to watch them use it.

Post-decisional depression. Once choices are made, clients may have second thoughts that keep them from acting on their decisions.

Acting too quickly. Some clients move into action too fast; liberated from the past, they find the first possibilities very attractive, skip the focus and direction of Task B, and go off half-cocked. Failing to weigh alternatives and shape goals often means repeating the process.

Culture. Wosket (2006) argues goal setting has cultural implications that helpers easily overlook. Objections are sometimes legitimately raised that Eurocentric, westernised approaches, the Skilled Helper model included, favour individual over collective goals, so counselors must avoid contaminating the client's process with their own bias toward dominant cultural norms. Goal setting can still apply in communal or collective contexts where allegiance to family or cultural expectations outweighs individual preference; committing to a course of action that honours duty is a legitimate goal. Her example: keeping the family together may matter more to an Irish Catholic woman, and give more fulfilment, than leaving an unsatisfying relationship.

Managing the shadow side. Effective helpers know what lurks in the shadows for themselves and clients and are ready to manage it. The answer lies in helpers being trained in the whole problem-management process and sharing a basic picture of it with clients, so that goal setting, in the client's language, becomes natural. Artful helpers weave goal setting into the flow of helping, moving between stages and tasks even in brief therapy.

King and Burton. In 'the hazards of goal pursuit' (2003), King and Burton note that research read one way suggests people should pursue goals that barely involve the self, are moderately important, fairly easy and moderately abstract, do not conflict and are not about money: in Egan's view, a boring life not worth living. Read another way, the research is a compendium of common mistakes in goal pursuit, nearly all of which violate principles in this chapter. Striving for goals is great but costly, so do it right. The authors do not advise avoiding goals because of pitfalls; the therapist's job is to help clients avoid or handle them. They conclude that only a hopelessly adolescent psychology would claim it is best to care about nothing to avoid disappointment.
sections.simple: Helpers and clients often dodge explicit goal setting: helpers are untrained, it feels too rational, the future is scary, it ends victimhood, it demands effort and it closes off options. Getting what you want brings new problems, post-decisional depression can stall action, and some clients rush in too fast. Goal setting must also respect collective, culture-based goals.
keyPoints: Bandura (1990): goal theory lacks the prominence it deserves; the main reason helpers skip goals is lack of training.
Reasons for avoidance: too rational, leaving the safe past, ending victimhood, self-demands, goals hem clients in.
Getting what you want brings new problems; post-decisional depression blocks action; some clients act too quickly.
Wosket (2006): beware individualist bias; duty-honouring collective goals are legitimate.
King and Burton (2003): hazards of goal pursuit are mostly violations of good goal-setting principles; caring about nothing is no answer.

terms.definition: The unnamed goals people operate with when they do not set goals explicitly; they may enhance or limit the person.
The system by which people direct their own behaviour; goals are a critical part of it, and client self-regulation is the ideal in helping.
The Stage II task of helping clients move from possibilities to choices, turning possibilities into a practical programme for change (innovation).
A concept: a specific statement about what a client wants and needs.
An accomplished goal.
An outcome that has a positive impact on the problem situation or opportunity.
Stating goals as results or patterns of behaviour in place by a certain time, rather than as activities.
Phrasing desired outcomes in completed form, e.g., 'drinking stopped', 'anger habitually controlled'.
A statement of intent to do something about a problem ('I need to do something about this'); a start that must be translated into aims and goals.
More than an intention: it has content, naming the area the client wants to work on and saying something general about it.
A clear, concrete pattern of behaviour the client wants to put in place.
A goal that serves as a strategy for reaching a higher-order goal (e.g., spending more time at home).
The end a set of instrumental goals serves (e.g., 'a good family life'); clients should be able to answer 'instrumental-for-what?'.
A goal that makes a significant contribution to managing the problem or developing the opportunity (is on target) and stretches the client.
A challenging goal; within reasonable limits, more challenging goals produce better performance.
Performance rises with difficulty only up to a point: goals too easy are ignored as trivial, goals too hard are not accepted.
A goal for which the client has access to the needed resources, which is under the client's control, and which external circumstances do not prevent.
A preliminary goal that must be met before the main goal can be pursued, e.g., Mara getting her father to commit to open dialogue.
A wise goal; Egan distinguishes prudence as playing it safe from prudence as doing the wise or even heroic thing.
A goal with staying power over a reasonable period, not merely achievable.
Ability to modify goals while keeping their purpose and to change tactics when a course is blocked or ineffective (Gollwitzer et al.).
Ability to stick with a goal or its means when the going gets rough.
Sticking with an original goal or action plan even when it is proving ineffective.
Gollwitzer and associates' recommended stance in goal pursuit, combining persistence with adaptability.
The criteria we use to make decisions; ethical helping respects them within reason.
Changes in attitudes and behaviours evident within the helping sessions themselves (Greenberg).
Changes in attitudes and behaviours that lead to further change (Greenberg).
Completion of the overall programme for constructive change through which problems are managed and opportunities developed (Greenberg).
Small sequenced goals set and executed early in helping (Taussig).
People who give their all to any task they undertake, such as Charles Colson.
What clients need may coincide with or differ from what they want; goals should address the package that makes sense for the client.
'Big, hairy, audacious goals': Collins and Porras's term for super-stretch goals; Egan thinks it fits business hype better than helping.
Modest goals that adapt to rather than change reality, often choosing a satisfactory alternative rather than the best.
Leahy's term for reluctance and resistance that set limits on change to reduce risk and uncertainty.
Leahy's term for the ways clients limit their own change (attacking the therapist, skipping homework, etc.).
Adjusting expectations without squashing hope; choosing adaptive rather than stretch goals.
Helping clients reframe a situation to see it in a positive light (Folkman and Moskowitz).
Helping clients deal with problems one at a time as they arise (Folkman and Moskowitz).

terms.term: Infusing ordinary events with positive meaning
terms.definition: Noting and valuing ordinary positive events that generate positive affect under stress (Folkman and Moskowitz).
Thoughts and actions used to handle difficulty: confronting, distancing, self-control, seeking social support, accepting responsibility.
Minor change: adjusting or fixing the current situation and dealing with symptoms.
Major change: changing the underlying system, transforming, based on new learning, a new narrative, attacking causes.
Goals that arise naturally through dialogue or everyday life rather than through explicit goal setting.
Helping clients commit themselves: 'What am I willing to pay for what I want?'; a dimension of goal setting rather than a sequential step.
Commitment to a goal versus continuing commitment to a strategy or plan to achieve it; initial commitment is proved by action.
Choosing goals that are worth more than they cost in work, time and emotional energy.
A tool (Chapter 13) for weighing costs against benefits in choosing goals and programmes.
A promise of a reward; a goal is appealing if there are incentives for pursuing it.
The highest form of commitment: the goal is the client's own, what the client really wants.
The least useful form of commitment: reluctantly going along with change.
A middle form of commitment based on reason ('this is logical'), which may lack staying power.
A contract clients make with themselves to behave in certain ways and attain goals; it also makes goals more focused.
Hidden conditions people unknowingly add to contracts ('until it begins to hurt').
Other things in clients' lives (job, family, leisure) that soak up time and energy needed for goals.
Bandura: beliefs in one's capabilities to organise and execute the courses of action required to manage prospective situations.
Clients' belief that their actions will most likely lead to desirable results.
Clients' belief that they have the wherewithal (knowledge, skills, time, stamina, guts) to carry out the needed behaviour.
Feedback based on deficiencies in performance, not in the client's personality.
Gollwitzer: intentions subordinate to goal intentions that specify when, where and how, in the form 'When situation x arises, I will perform response y!'.
Second thoughts after choices are made that keep clients from acting on their decisions.

practice.q: Discuss the flexible guidelines Egan offers for helping clients set goals for themselves.
practice.answer:
Introduction. In Stage II of Egan's Skilled Helper model, Task II-B helps clients move from possibilities to choices, turning the creative output of Task II-A into a practical programme for change. Egan stresses that practical goals rarely appear fully formed; they must be 'designed' through dialogue. He defines goals as specific statements of what clients want and need, and lists characteristics that make goals workable, illustrating each with Mara and her father. He then turns these into flexible principles.

1. Describe the future in outcome or accomplishment language. Helping is about problem-managing outcomes, not activities. 'Start doing some exercise' is an activity; 'running three miles in under 30 minutes four times a week within six months' is an outcome. The past-participle approach (drinking stopped, fights decreased) helps clients avoid directionless action and work smarter, as when Laura helped Karl turn 'more disciplined' into a regular sleep schedule.

2. Move from broad aims to clear and specific goals. Clients progress from good intentions ('I need to do something') to broad aims with content ('spend more time with my family') to specific goals ('three weekends a month at home'). Instrumental goals serve ultimate goals, so helpers ask 'instrumental-for-what?'. Specific goals have the best chance and make progress verifiable, though clients should not get lost in detail.

3. Establish goals that make a difference. Goals have substance if they are on target, as with Vittorio and Anthony's marketing-department deal, and if they stretch clients. Locke and Latham found that within limits harder goals produce better performance, though the relationship is curvilinear: too easy is ignored, too hard is rejected.

4. Formulate realistic goals. A goal is realistic if resources are available (Rory moving from consulting to design supervision), it is under the client's control (Tony controlling his reactions, not his parents), and external circumstances do not block it. Mara needed a pre-goal: her father's commitment to dialogue.

5. Set prudent goals. Realistic is not prudent. Harry's leap into an ambitious dating programme ended in rehospitalisation; bite-size goals in the same direction worked. Egan favours prudence as wise or heroic choice rather than playing safe.

6. Set sustainable goals. A couple who reunited and divorced again in six months had an achievable but unsustainable goal; AA's one-day-at-a-time approach shows how to build staying power.

7. Choose goals with flexibility. In uncertain situations goals must adapt, as with Jessie's interim goal of preparing for a new career. Gollwitzer and colleagues distinguish flexibility, tenacity and rigidity, recommending flexible tenacity.

8. Choose goals consistent with values. Values are decision criteria; helping is ethical only if it respects them. Vincente and Consuela were helped to clarify their values about their son's life support; Karl used his values to balance study and work.

9. Establish realistic time frames. Goals for 'sometime' rarely happen. Greenberg's immediate, intermediate and final outcomes (Janette, Jensen), Taussig's early mini goals, and now, soon, short-term and long-term goals (the accused priest) give structure.

Conclusion. Egan insists these are tools, not a step-by-step formula; not every goal needs every characteristic. Skilled helpers keep them in mind and use them as timely 'sculpting' probes, helping clients build goals with agency built in, using questions like those in Box 12.1.

practice.q: What is Task II-C? Explain the strategies counselors use to help clients commit themselves to their goals.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Task II-C asks clients, "What am I willing to pay for what I want?" Egan cites Tickell's observation that there is optimism about human ability to cope but pessimism about the will to do so. Clients may set goals without being willing to pay for them; once goals are stated, the 'old self' competes with the potential 'new self'. Egan stresses that II-C is a dimension of goal setting rather than a sequential step. Counselors should not push clients to heroic efforts but should not undersell them either, as the dying mother who lived to see her son's wedding shows. Key questions include whether the goal is worth it, where to invest limited time, money and energy, and how strong competing agendas are.

Initial and ongoing commitment. Initial commitment to a goal differs from ongoing commitment to a plan. Its proof lies in action, as with the client whose nightly 'examination of conscience' revealed contempt beneath his abrasiveness.

1. Economics: goals worth more than they cost. Some achievable goals cost too much. Skilled counselors help clients budget work, time and emotional energy. Eunice declined treatments that would only prolong a low-quality life and chose hospice care. Because cost-benefit ratios are hard to calculate, the key is helping clients foresee consequences; a woman who abruptly stopped chemotherapy without exploring consequences later regretted it. The balance-sheet method can help.

2. Incentives: appealing goals. Useful goals are not automatically appealing. An incentive is a promise of a reward and builds hope. Negative goals should be translated into positive ones: Karl found 'throwing away the crutch and walking straight' and earning a degree far more appealing than simply giving up drugs.

3. Ownership: embracing goals. Goals must be the client's own. Carl Rogers returned responsibility to a client by asking what she wanted him to tell her to do; Cynthia's lawyer made her 'start from zero' rather than follow her in-laws' custody suggestion. Others' goals let clients blame others and skip consequences. Commitment ranges from compliance (least useful), to buy-in (reason-based, may lack staying power), to ownership ('this is mine'). A resistant manager moved through all three over two years as he found incentives.

Contracts. Self-contracts are promises to oneself that also focus goals. Dora, after her son's disappearance, used a series of contracts to reopen her life and recommit to her other son, acting herself into new thinking. Contracts are human instruments, not legal documents, but they can carry covert codicils such as 'until it begins to hurt'.

4. Obstacles: competing agendas. Job, family and leisure soak up time and energy; one manager achieved none of his self-development goals because of business pressure and divorce. Change often requires reordering priorities or compromises, and sometimes choosing between right and right, as for a two-career couple planning a child. Box 12.2 offers questions to test commitment, such as readiness, appeal, free choice, incentives and support.

Conclusion. Commitment is where goals meet real costs. By attending to economics, incentives, ownership and competing agendas, and using tools like contracts and Box 12.2, counselors help clients face up to their commitments and move toward action.

practice.q: Explain the concept of self-efficacy and describe how counselors can help clients develop it, as discussed by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan regards client self-regulation as the ideal: the more clients find motivation within themselves, the better. Following Galassi and Bruch, the counselor's role is to help clients choose goals, commit to them and develop agency and assertiveness. Expectations also matter, and Egan examines them through Bandura's concept of self-efficacy. He notes that claims for self-concepts have been questioned by recent research, while Swann and colleagues argue self-views do matter; Egan sides with those who find self-efficacy clinically very useful, even if it is not 'pure' evidence-wise.

Nature of self-efficacy. Bandura defines perceived self-efficacy as beliefs in one's capabilities to organise and execute the actions needed to manage prospective situations. These beliefs affect how people think, feel, motivate themselves and act: their willingness to try, how much effort they spend and how long they persist. Clients with higher self-efficacy make bolder choices. Clients act when two conditions hold: outcome expectations (the action will likely lead to desired results) and self-efficacy beliefs (I have the knowledge, skills, time, stamina and guts to do it). Yolanda, after a stroke, had both and progressed well in rehabilitation. Yves believed he could finish drug rehabilitation but doubted it would lead anywhere ('drug-free for what?'). Xavier believed treatment would help but doubted his stamina and courage. Both refused. These concepts apply in education, health, rehabilitation and work.

Developing self-efficacy. Egan illustrates with Nick, a strong manager doubtful he could change his abrasive style.
1. Skills: ensure clients have needed skills. Nick attended sessions on listening, empathic highlights, feedback and challenge, reawakening dormant skills. Skills must be acquired in a way that gives a sense of competence.
2. Corrective feedback: target performance, not personality. Egan told Nick he need not respond positively to every idea but should sort and explain; feedback that feels like a personality attack harms self-efficacy.
3. Positive feedback: make it as specific as corrective feedback, using the formula: what you did, its positive outcome, and its wider upbeat impact, rather than a perfunctory 'nice job'.
4. Success as reinforcer: small successes, like Nick's successful delegation, build courage for harder tasks, but success must be linked to a sense of increased competence.
5. Models: learning from others builds competence. Nick realised the manager he most admired was excellent with people, though pride made modelling tricky.
6. Encouragement: support must be real and tailored, not patronising; Egan's encouragement of Nick was subtle and indirect.
7. Reducing fear and anxiety: fear of failure blocks action. Nick's fears of harming the business and looking foolish faded as results held and he recognised his upbeat style with field teams.

Conclusion. Self-efficacy, the 'I can, I will' belief, joins outcome expectations as a condition for action. Egan emphasises that these strategies are things helpers can do, not must do, and that each helper must develop a personal style; no single style is right.

practice.q: Discuss Egan's views on what kind of change clients need and how much, with reference to needs and wants, adaptive goals, coping and second-order change.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan holds that therapy should be client driven: the degree of change is in the client's hands. Trivial goals should be avoided, but a complete personality makeover is unrealistic, though Charles Colson's radical life change shows that '100 percenters' exist. Most change falls between minor upsets and such transformations. Egan explores this through four themes.

Needs versus wants. Asking 'what kind of change does the client need?' helps answer 'how much?'. Wants and needs may coincide (a lonely person wants and needs community) or differ. Goals should target the package of needs and wants that makes sense for the client. Irv, with a heart condition and MS, had to move painfully from the lifestyle he wanted to the one he needed. Involuntary clients, like the homeless woman who wanted freedom from responsibility, may need challenge to look beyond wants, though the decision remains theirs. Milos, a refugee, integrated his want for homeland ties with his need to integrate, and his depression lifted.

Adaptive goals. Collins and Porras's BHAGs suit business hype more than helping; even big goals need a bit-by-bit approach. Wheeler and Janis caution that searching for the absolute best can cost more than it gains; a satisfactory alternative may be wiser. Joyce gained some freedom from her demanding mother without restructuring the relationship, making life 'a little bit better'. Leahey and Wallace's client decided enough self-esteem was good enough, and some couples accept surface solutions. Leahy calls resistance 'strategic self-limitation' or self-handicapping, a way to limit risk; helpers may point it out but should not impose goals. Helping clients adapt rather than conquer is not failure.

Coping. Coping means adjusting expectations without squashing hope, and adaptive goals are associated with it. Everyone copes at times; often it is cope or succumb. A widowed mother 'coping well' shows its upside. Folkman and Moskowitz suggest generating positive affect through positive reappraisal (Victor separating his rehabilitation goal from its arduous steps), problem-focused coping (Agnes handling each caregiving problem as it comes), and infusing ordinary events with positive meaning (over 99% of AIDS caregivers recalled such events). Clients also need coping skills, such as confronting, distancing, self-control, seeking support and accepting responsibility, and flexibility in using them.

Second-order change. This concerns the size of change, with coping at the other end. Singhal, Rao and Pant contrast first-order change (adjusting, motoring on, fixing, old learning, old narrative, fiddling with symptoms) with second-order change (changing the system, creating something new, transforming, new learning, new narrative, attacking causes). The literature often treats only second-order change as 'real', but Egan sees a continuum where first-order change has uses and may be the only option. Mara may choose major or minor change; Algis and Rodaina's reduced squabbling is first-order, while redefining their relationship would be closer to second-order.

Conclusion. How much change? It depends. Clients are in the driver's seat, and the helper's knowledge of goal setting and change serves to help them make life-enhancing choices that suit them.

practice.q: Critically discuss the shadow side of goal setting as described by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan presents goal setting as powerful, supported by research such as Locke and Latham's. Yet he notes that helpers and clients often seem to conspire to avoid explicit goal setting; counselors explore problems and stop short of asking clients what they want. Bandura remarked that goal theory has not received the prominence its evidence deserves, and Bronfenbrenner recalled a Russian psychologist contrasting American interest in how a child came to be with Soviet interest in what the child can become.

Reasons helpers and clients avoid goals.
First, lack of training: a main reason counselors do not help clients set goals is that they are not trained to.
Second, goal setting seems too rational; clients' lives are messy and goal setting feels sterile and alien, even though many would benefit from rigorous problem management. This is a real dilemma.
Third, goal setting moves clients from the relatively safe harbour of discussing problems and their roots in the past into the uncharted waters of the future, uncomfortable for both parties.
Fourth, setting and committing to goals ends the victim-of-my-problems game; victimhood and self-responsibility do not mix.
Fifth, goals place demands on clients: saying 'this is what I want' implies committing to action and paying the price, so clients are not always grateful.
Sixth, goals hem clients in; choosing one path closes others, such as a career limiting the kind of marriage possible.

Problems after choosing. The ironic saying that getting what you want is worse than not getting it holds some truth: a drug-free life, renewed marriage or promotion brings responsibilities and new problems; even good solutions create problems, as parents who grant freedom then watch children use it. Post-decisional depression, second thoughts after choosing, can keep clients from acting. Conversely, some clients rush into action, attracted by the first possibilities, skip Task B and go off half-cocked, often having to redo the process.

Cultural considerations. Wosket points out that goal setting has overlooked cultural implications. Eurocentric approaches, including the Skilled Helper model, may favour individual over collective goals, and counselors must not contaminate clients' processes with bias toward dominant norms. Goal setting still applies in collective contexts; honouring duty is a legitimate goal, as when keeping the family together matters more to an Irish Catholic woman than leaving an unsatisfying relationship.

Managing the shadow side. Effective helpers know these shadows in themselves and clients. The remedy is training in the whole problem-management process and sharing its basic picture with clients, so goal setting, in the client's language, becomes natural and is woven into helping, even in brief therapy.

Critical evaluation: King and Burton. Their 'hazards of goal pursuit' suggests, read one way, that people should pursue only modest, easy, non-conflicting, non-financial goals that barely involve the self, which Egan calls a boring life. Read another way, it catalogues mistakes that mostly violate the chapter's principles. Goal striving is costly, so it must be done right; the helper's job is to help clients avoid pitfalls, not avoid goals.

Conclusion. The shadow side does not argue against goal setting but for skilled, culturally sensitive goal setting, since only a hopelessly adolescent psychology would recommend caring about nothing to avoid disappointment.

practice.q: Explain the four ways in which goal setting empowers clients.
practice.answer:
Egan, drawing on Locke and Latham's 2002 review of 35 years of research, describes four ways goals empower clients.

1. Goals focus attention. Simon, a torture survivor, seemed aimless until asked what he wanted most; he said 'a friend' and stayed focused, revealing loneliness as his core concern.

2. Goals mobilise energy and direct effort. Lethargic clients often come alive when discussing a better future. A listless rehabilitation patient who decided God and creation, not pain, would be central to her life began cooperating fully with exercises. Even rudimentary goals can trigger constructive change.

3. Goals provide incentives to search for strategies. Goal setting (Stage II) leads naturally into searching for means (Stage III). Lonnie, after a heart scare, found ingenious ways to rebuild her social life, such as taking in student boarders.

4. Clear and specific goals increase persistence. An AIDS patient recovered from five hospitalisations to be reintegrated into his family. Payne, Robbins and Dougherty found high-goal-directed retirees more outgoing, resourceful and persistent than low-goal-directed ones.

Egan adds that even not setting goals leaves covert default goals, so it makes sense to make goals work for clients.

practice.q: Distinguish between instrumental and ultimate goals, and explain the movement from good intentions to specific goals.
practice.answer:
Egan describes goal shaping as a progression. A good intention ('I need to do something about this') is a start but lacks content. A broad aim identifies the area and says something general, as when Jon decides he must spend more time with his family. A specific goal describes a clear pattern of behaviour: Jon will spend three of four weekends at home and work no more than two evenings a week. The counselor then probes quality, not just quantity. A bickering couple similarly moves from 'straighten out our marriage' to 'handle finances constructively' to a monthly budget and fewer fights.

Instrumental versus ultimate goals. An ultimate or higher-order goal is the end sought, such as Jon's 'good family life', which differs across families and cultures. An instrumental goal, such as spending more time at home, is a strategy that serves it. Because instrumental goals serve higher-order ones, helpers should check clients can answer the 'instrumental-for-what?' question. Some goals are both: a household budget is a goal in itself and instrumental to peace at home.

Specific goals have the best chance and make progress verifiable, though clients should not get lost in planning details.

practice.q: Describe compliance, buy-in and ownership as forms of commitment to goals.
practice.answer:
Egan stresses that goals must be the client's own, not the helper's or anyone else's; goals chosen by others let clients blame others and skip exploring consequences. Carl Rogers returned responsibility by asking a client what she wanted him to tell her to do.

Commitment takes three forms:
- Compliance is the least useful: grudgingly accepting change ('I guess I'll have to change some habits to keep my marriage afloat'). It bodes poorly for sustained change, though it may be better than nothing.
- Buy-in is a level up: the client sees the changes as essential and logical. But it can lack staying power because it relies on reason; 'this is logical' differs from 'this is what I really want'.
- Ownership is the highest form: the goal is not someone else's or just a good idea; it is what the client wants.

Egan's example is a manager told to change his style. He first called it 'hogwash', but complied when he realised it would cost little. Positive responses from his team brought buy-in ('the right thing to do'). A year later he became proactive and found it fun: ownership. The process took over two years, driven by meaningful incentives rather than personality change.

practice.q: What are implementation intentions? How do they help clients move to action?
practice.answer:
Egan notes that commitment to goals is not enough; it must be matched by commitment to the actions needed, the work of Stage III. Gollwitzer and associates researched a simple way to overcome common problems in translating goals into action, such as failing to start, distraction and reverting to old habits.

Gollwitzer argues good intentions do not deserve their bad reputation: strong intentions are reliably realised more often than weak ones. Implementation intentions are subordinate to goal intentions and specify the when, where and how of goal-directed responses, in the form 'When situation x arises, I will perform response y!'. They link anticipated opportunities to chosen responses.

Gwendolyn, a nursing-home aide, resolves that when Enid becomes abusive she will not respond immediately, will remind herself it is the illness talking, and then respond with patience and kindness. She refreshes this intention often, and her responses become almost automatic: the patient's behaviour becomes a cue, even an 'opportunity', for the desired response. Similarly, a person managing weight automatically looks for the right food on a restaurant menu.

Helpers can help clients state such strong, specific intentions, which have great practical value for turning goals into accomplishments.

practice.q: Explain Folkman and Moskowitz's three ways of generating positive affect in coping.
practice.answer:
Egan treats coping as an important goal, defining it, after an Economist remark, as adjusting expectations without squashing hope. Folkman and Moskowitz see positive affect as central to coping and suggest three ways counselors can help clients generate and sustain it under chronic stress.

1. Positive reappraisal: reframing a situation positively. Victor saw his rehabilitation after a motorcycle accident as 'one big daunting glob'. His counselor helped him picture the end state and separate it from the arduous steps, so he coped with part of it each day and saw weekly progress.

2. Problem-focused coping: dealing with problems one at a time. Agnes, caring for her husband with MS, did not have to cope with 'his MS' as a whole but with specific, near-at-hand caregiving tasks. Her sense of mastery brought positive affect.

3. Infusing ordinary events with positive meaning. In their study of AIDS caregivers, more than 99% described an ordinary event, like dinner with a friend, flowers or a compliment, that made them feel good and helped them through the day.

Egan adds that coping assumes clients have coping skills and the flexibility to fit them to situations; otherwise helpers coach or teach them.

practice.q: Describe Greenberg's classification of outcomes and the use of time frames in goal setting.
practice.answer:
Egan notes that goals to be achieved 'sometime or other' probably will not be achieved, so time frames add value. Greenberg distinguished three outcomes:
- Immediate outcomes: changes in attitudes and behaviours evident within sessions. Janette, who wanted to stop being passive, practised assertiveness safely with her counselor.
- Intermediate outcomes: changes leading to further change. Janette gradually transferred assertiveness to safe real-life situations, such as standing up to her mother.
- Final outcomes: completion of the overall change programme. Janette took over two years to become consistently assertive.

Jensen, on probation for shoplifting, showed the same pattern: an immediate working alliance with his counselor; an intermediate change in his entitlement attitude; and final outcomes of completing probation without reoffending and holding a job to repay the retailer.

Taussig highlighted the value of early, sequenced mini goals. Egan also notes goals may be 'now', 'soon', short-term or long-term, as for a priest unjustly accused of child molestation: relief from anxiety, legal aid, winning the case, and rebuilding credibility. There is no formula; helping remains an art.

practice.q: Differentiate between first-order and second-order change.

practice.answer: A pre-goal is a preliminary goal that must be achieved before the main goal can be pursued. Mara cannot change her father's attitudes, only influence them, so Carlos helps her see that her pre-goal is to get her father to commit to reasonably open dialogue before she can negotiate a new role.

Flexible tenacity is the stance recommended by Gollwitzer and associates for goal pursuit. It combines tenacity (sticking with a goal when the going gets rough) with flexibility (modifying goals or tactics while keeping their purpose), and avoids rigidity (clinging to an ineffective goal or plan).

Robert Leahy's term for reluctant and resistant behaviours, such as attacking the therapist or skipping homework, that set limits on change. Because change brings risk and uncertainty, clients put up barriers, in effect saying 'enough is enough'. Helpers may point out this self-handicapping but should not impose goals.

Post-decisional depression, discussed in the shadow side of goal setting, is the phenomenon in which clients, after making choices, begin to have second thoughts that often keep them from acting on their decisions.

practice.q: What are BHAGs? What is Egan's view of them?
practice.answer: BHAGs, 'big, hairy, audacious goals', is Collins and Porras's term for super-stretch goals. Egan thinks the term fits business hype more than helping; even clients with big goals need a bit-by-bit approach, dividing them into smaller pieces so they do not seem daunting.

practice.q: Distinguish outcome expectations from self-efficacy beliefs.
practice.answer: Outcome expectations are clients' beliefs that an action will likely lead to desired results. Self-efficacy beliefs are their conviction that they have the wherewithal (skills, knowledge, time, stamina, guts) to carry out that action. Clients tend to act when both are present; Yves lacked the first, Xavier the second.

summary: Everyone sets goals; not naming them leaves covert default goals. Locke and Latham's research shows goals focus attention, mobilise energy, prompt strategy search and increase persistence.
Task II-B moves clients from possibilities (creativity) to choices (innovation). A goal is a concept, an outcome is an accomplished goal, and a problem-managing outcome has positive impact.
Workable goals are outcome-stated, specific, substantive, venturesome yet prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, value-congruent and time-framed; these are tools, not a formula.
Goals move from good intentions to broad aims to specific goals; instrumental goals serve ultimate goals ('instrumental-for-what?'), and clear goals make progress verifiable.
Substantive goals are on target and stretching; difficulty and performance relate curvilinearly. Realistic goals need resources, client control and no blocking circumstances; pre-goals may be needed.
Prudent goals are wise (sometimes heroic), sustainable goals have staying power, and flexible goals adapt; Gollwitzer recommends flexible tenacity over rigidity.
Goals must respect client values; time frames (Greenberg's immediate, intermediate and final outcomes; Taussig's mini goals; now/soon/short/long-term) add agency.
The amount of change is client driven: distinguish needs from wants, consider adaptive goals and satisfactory alternatives, and respect strategic self-limitation.
Coping, adjusting expectations without squashing hope, is a worthy goal; Folkman and Moskowitz suggest positive reappraisal, problem-focused coping and positive meaning in ordinary events.
First-order change adjusts; second-order change transforms the system. Egan sees a continuum and leaves the choice to clients.
Goals may emerge naturally, but explicit early goal setting is also effective (Taussig).

Task II-C ('What am I willing to pay?') is a dimension of goal setting: help clients make goals worth their cost, appealing, owned (compliance to buy-in to ownership) and protected from competing agendas; self-contracts help but carry covert codicils.
Self-efficacy (Bandura) plus outcome expectations drive action; it is built through skills, performance-based and specific positive feedback, success, models, genuine encouragement and reducing fear.
Each Stage II task can trigger action, and implementation intentions ('When x, I will y') help translate goals into action.

The shadow side: helpers lack training, goal setting seems too rational, scary or demanding, goals hem clients in, getting what you want brings new problems, post-decisional depression and hasty action occur, and cultural bias toward individual goals must be avoided.

assessment.q: Locke and Latham's 2002 American Psychologist article summarised how many years of goal-setting research?
assessment.explain: They summarised 35 years of empirical research on goal setting.

assessment.q: Simon, the torture survivor, became focused when asked what one thing he wanted. His answer was:
assessment.explain: Simon said 'A friend'; loneliness was uppermost in his mind, illustrating that goals focus attention.

assessment.q: Lonnie's ingenious redevelopment of her social life after a heart scare illustrates that goals:
assessment.explain: Setting goals leads naturally to a search for means of accomplishing them.
options: Provide incentives to search for strategies
Should be avoided in old age

assessment.q: Of the four options Bea considered for dealing with anger, she chose:
assessment.explain: She channelled her anger by joining a political action group.

assessment.q: 'I'm going to consistently spend three out of four weekends a month at home' is an example of a:
assessment.explain: It is a specific pattern of behaviour, although it addresses quantity rather than quality.

assessment.q: Rory's shift from consulting to a supervisory role in graphic design illustrates the realism criterion of:
assessment.explain: He lacked the resources for consulting but had those needed for the design supervisory role.

assessment.q: Tony, the 16-year-old caught between his parents, was helped to:
assessment.explain: Goals should be under the client's control; Tony could control his reactions.
options: Control his own reactions rather than his parents' behaviour

assessment.q: Jessie's interim goal of preparing for a job outside his industry illustrates goals that are:
assessment.explain: His counselor helped him choose a more flexible interim goal suited to a recession-hit industry.

assessment.q: Who distinguished immediate, intermediate and final outcomes?
assessment.explain: Greenberg (1986) described these three types of outcomes.

assessment.q: 'Big, hairy, audacious goals' (BHAGs) was coined by:
assessment.explain: Collins and Porras (1994) coined the term for super-stretch goals.

assessment.q: Joyce's case is an example of:
assessment.explain: Counselling made her life 'a little bit better', an adaptive goal.
options: Choosing a satisfactory alternative rather than the best

assessment.q: Egan uses the Economist's comment on Condoleezza Rice, 'adjust expectations without squashing hope', as a definition of:
assessment.explain: Egan says it is not a bad definition of coping.

assessment.q: Victor's counselor helping him separate the desirable end state from the arduous rehabilitation activities illustrates:
assessment.explain: Positive reappraisal reframes a situation to see it in a positive light.

assessment.q: Reducing the frequency and intensity of Algis and Rodaina's squabbling 'smacks of':
assessment.explain: Changing the style and terms of the relationship would be closer to second-order change.

assessment.q: Carl Rogers's question 'What is it that you want me to tell you to do?' puts responsibility for goal setting on:
assessment.explain: It places responsibility for goal setting on the client's shoulders, supporting ownership.

assessment.q: The manager whose style changed took how long to move from resistance to ownership?
assessment.explain: The process took over two years.

assessment.explain: Box 12.2 lists questions to test commitment; Box 12.1 is for choosing and shaping goals.
